appellations.name: Arnad-Montjovet
appellations.grapes: Nebbiolo (min 70%), plus Dolcetto, Vien de Nus, Pinot Noir, Freisa
appellations.summary: Nebbiolo-based reds from the lower valley around Arnad and Montjovet, near the Fort of Bard. Light, fragrant and mountain-edged.
appellations.terroir: Granite terraces on steep slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Arnad is also famous for its lard (Lardo d'Arnad DOP), cured in chestnut-wood tubs.

appellations.name: Donnas
appellations.summary: The first DOC of the valley (1971) and the gateway from Piedmont. Nebbiolo here, called Picotendro, grows on pergolas over granite terraces that continue straight into Carema. The wines are pale, firm and fragrant, aged at least two years. The Caves Coopératives de Donnas, founded in 1971, makes nearly all of it.
appellations.terroir: Granite and gneiss terraces at 300 to 600 m, with stone pillars and pergolas like Carema's.
appellations.nerd_note: The vineyards line the Roman Via delle Gallie, which was hacked through the rock at Donnas around the first century BC; a Roman milestone arch still stands in the cutting.

appellations.name: Cinque Terre
appellations.summary:
The five fishing villages of Monterosso, Vernazza, Corniglia, Manarola and Riomaggiore cling to cliffs on the coast west of La Spezia, and above them rises one of the most dramatic vineyard landscapes in the world: about 7,000 km of dry-stone terraces built over a thousand years. The UNESCO World Heritage listing (1997, with Portovenere and the islands) recognises this landscape, and the national park works to stop it collapsing back into scrub.

The dry white Cinque Terre DOC, mostly Bosco with Albarola and Vermentino, is herbal, saline and crisp. The treasure is Sciacchetrà: the same grapes dried on racks for about two months, then pressed into a tiny quantity of amber, apricot-and-honey sweet wine aged at least a year (Riserva three). Grapes are carried down by hand or by small monorail trains (*trenini a cremagliera*). Production is tiny, under 100 hectares in total, and the Cantina Cinque Terre cooperative at Groppo makes much of it, alongside growers like Possa (Heydi Bonanini), Walter De Batté and Buranco.
appellations.terroir: Sandstone (macigno) and shale on slopes up to 45 degrees, often dropping straight to the sea; terraces face south-west into the sun and sea breeze.
appellations.nerd_note: Sciacchetrà's name is often explained as dialect for 'crush' (*sciacca*) and 'set aside' (*tra*), describing pressing the dried grapes and keeping the precious wine.

appellations.name: Rossese di Dolceacqua
appellations.summary: Liguria's first DOC and its most distinctive red, from the Nervia and Verbone valleys behind Ventimiglia near the French border. Rossese (which DNA links to Tibouren of Provence) gives a pale, perfumed, spicy red with wild strawberry, rose and sea-salt notes, sometimes compared to a Mediterranean Pinot Noir. Steep terraces and old alberello vines are the norm, and in 2012 the disciplinare recognised named vineyard sites (menzioni geografiche) such as Posaú, Galeae, Beragna and Arcagna. Maccario Dringenberg, Terre Bianche, Ka*Manciné and Testalonga are reference producers.
appellations.terroir: Steep terraces of marl and sandstone (flysch) at 150 to 600 m in the hinterland of the Riviera dei Fiori.
appellations.nerd_note: Legend says Napoleon tasted Rossese at Dolceacqua and declared it fit for an emperor, and Pope Paul III is also said to have praised it in the 16th century.

appellations.name: Riviera ligure di Ponente
appellations.grapes: Pigato, Vermentino, Rossese, Ormeasco (Dolcetto), Granaccia, Moscato
appellations.summary: The umbrella DOC for the western Riviera from Ventimiglia to Genoa, best known for Pigato and Vermentino. Pigato, whose name refers to the freckles (*pighe*) on its ripe skins, is especially at home in the Albenga plain and its valleys (Arroscia, Lerrone, Neva), where it makes rich, herbal, slightly bitter whites with notes of peach, rosemary and resin; genetically it is the same as Vermentino, but growers stand by its distinct character. Subzones include Riviera dei Fiori, Albenganese, Finalese and Quiliano, plus Taggia for Moscato and Granaccia from Quiliano.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial and clay-limestone soils in the Albenga valleys; terraced flysch and limestone near Finale and Imperia.
appellations.nerd_note: Albenga's plain is an island of flat land in Liguria, and Pigato from Ortovero and Ranzo is where the variety's reputation was built from the 1980s.

appellations.name: Colli di Luni
appellations.grapes: Vermentino (min 90% for Vermentino), Sangiovese, Ciliegiolo, Canaiolo
appellations.summary: A DOC straddling the Liguria-Tuscany border around Sarzana and the Magra valley, named after the Roman port of Luna. Its Vermentino is the richest and most structured in Liguria, with ripe citrus, almond and Mediterranean herbs, closer to the Tuscan coastal style. Vermentino 'Superiore' and reds based on Sangiovese and Ciliegiolo exist. Lunae Bosoni, Ottaviano Lambruschi (Costa Marina, Sarticola), La Baia del Sole and Giacomelli are leaders.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial terraces of the Magra plus hillside clays and marls around Castelnuovo Magra and Ortonovo; warm and protected by the Apuan Alps.
appellations.nerd_note: Luni's Roman wine was praised by Pliny the Elder; the ruins of the Roman town, abandoned in the Middle Ages because of malaria, lie a few kilometres from today's vineyards.

appellations.name: Colline di Levanto
appellations.summary: A tiny DOC on the terraces just north of the Cinque Terre around Levanto, Bonassola and Framura, making light coastal Vermentino-based whites and Sangiovese reds.
appellations.terroir: Shale and sandstone terraces above the sea.
appellations.nerd_note: Levanto's terraces are the northern continuation of the Cinque Terre landscape.

appellations.name: Golfo del Tigullio - Portofino
appellations.grapes: Vermentino, Bianchetta Genovese, Moscato, Ciliegiolo, Dolcetto
appellations.summary: The DOC of the Tigullio gulf from Portofino to Sestri Levante and inland valleys. Bianchetta Genovese, a delicate local white, and Ciliegiolo reds are its specialities.
appellations.terroir: Shale and sandstone hills behind the gulf.
appellations.nerd_note: Bisson ages a sparkling wine, Abissi, at the bottom of the sea in the Portofino marine park.

appellations.name: Val Polcèvera
appellations.grapes: Vermentino, Bianchetta Genovese, Albarola; Dolcetto, Sangiovese, Ciliegiolo
appellations.summary: A small DOC in the valley behind Genoa. The Coronata subzone, once a famous suburban vineyard of the city, survives in fragments among the industrial outskirts.
appellations.terroir: Clay and serpentine slopes behind the port of Genoa.
appellations.nerd_note: Coronata white was a classic match for Genoese fish dishes in the 19th century.

appellations.name: Pornassio
appellations.summary: The DOC of Ormeasco, Liguria's name for Dolcetto, in the mountains around Pornassio in the upper Arroscia valley. The grape reportedly arrived from Piedmont in the 14th century. Reds, Superiore, a rosé called Sciac-trà (not to be confused with Sciacchetrà) and passito are made.
appellations.terroir: Mountain slopes at 400 to 800 m on the border with Piedmont.
appellations.nerd_note: The Ormeasco Sciac-trà rosé shares its dialect name, meaning 'crush and draw off', with the Cinque Terre's sweet wine.

appellations.name: Franciacorta
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Nero, Pinot Bianco (max 50%), Erbamat (max 10%)
appellations.summary:
Franciacorta is Italy's most prestigious traditional-method sparkling wine and the first Italian sparkling DOCG to require bottle fermentation. The zone covers 19 communes on the hills south of Lake Iseo, west of Brescia, with 3,634 hectares of vineyard in 2025 and about 19 million bottles shipped in 2024, overwhelmingly to Italian customers (only about 12% is exported).

The modern story begins in 1961, when the young winemaker Franco Ziliani convinced Guido Berlucchi, a local nobleman who made a dull still white, to let him try a Champagne-method sparkler: 3,000 bottles of 'Pinot di Franciacorta' went on sale and sold out. Franciacorta became a DOC in 1967, Maurizio Zanella founded Ca' del Bosco in the 1970s, Vittorio Moretti founded Bellavista, and in 1995 Franciacorta became a DOCG. Since 2003 the name 'Franciacorta' alone on the label (no 'metodo classico', no 'spumante') is the denomination, a deliberate imitation of Champagne.

Rules are stricter than Champagne's in places: non-vintage wines age at least 18 months on the lees (25 months from harvest), Satèn (a blanc de blancs of Chardonnay and Pinot Bianco at lower pressure, under 5 atmospheres) 24 months, Millesimato 30 months and Riserva 60 months. Rosé must include at least 35% Pinot Nero. Erbamat, an ancient late-ripening local white recorded since the 16th century, was admitted in 2017 to bring acidity as summers warm. The consortium has since halted new vineyard plantings until 2028 to protect prices.
appellations.terroir: The hills are an amphitheatre of glacial moraine, left by the glacier that carved Lake Iseo, with six soil types identified in a 1992 University of Milan zoning: deep fluvio-glacial gravels, fine colluvial soils, and calcareous rock on Monte Orfano. The lake moderates temperatures and the Alps to the north block cold air, so the grapes ripen fully but keep acidity; warming summers are pushing harvests into early August.
appellations.nerd_note: Franciacorta was the first wine region in Italy whose consortium made the denomination name alone mandatory, banning the word 'spumante' from the label to put itself on a par with Champagne.

appellations.name: Curtefranca
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay and Pinot Bianco (white); Cabernet Franc, Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot (red)
appellations.summary: The still-wine DOC of the Franciacorta zone, renamed from Terre di Franciacorta in 2008 to avoid confusion with the sparkling DOCG. Bordeaux-style reds and Chardonnay whites; Ca' del Bosco's Maurizio Zanella red started here.
appellations.terroir: Moraine hills south of Lake Iseo.
appellations.nerd_note: Franciacorta's Cabernet Franc plantings include old vines later identified as Carmenère, as happened in north-east Italy.

appellations.name: Valtellina Superiore
appellations.summary:
Valtellina is Nebbiolo's mountain home, an Alpine valley along the Adda river just south of Switzerland where vines grow on about 2,500 km of dry-stone terraces stacked up the south-facing slope of the Rhaetian Alps, between 300 and 800 metres. Valtellina Superiore ages at least 24 months (12 in wood) and 36 for Riserva, and is lighter, more transparent and more mineral than Barolo, with rose, red currant, herbs and a slatey bite.

Five historic subzones run west to east along the valley and may appear on the label: Maroggia (the smallest, near Berbenno), Sassella (west of Sondrio around the Santuario della Madonna della Sassella, warm and rocky, often called the finest), Grumello (named after the ruined Castel Grumello above Montagna), Inferno (a small, steep, hot 'inferno' of rock east of Sondrio around Poggiridenti) and Valgella (the largest, around Teglio and Chiuro). Wine bottled in Switzerland may carry the name 'Stagafassli', a legacy of the centuries when Valtellina belonged to the Grisons.

Total vineyard area in the valley is about 850 hectares today, versus roughly 6,000 in the mid-19th century. Producers such as Arpepe, Nino Negri, Sandro Fay, Mamete Prevostini, Aldo Rainoldi, Dirupi and Barbacàn have made it one of the most exciting Nebbiolo zones in Italy.
appellations.terroir: Granite, gneiss and schist weathered into thin sandy soils (often carried up the terraces by hand), with high acidity and excellent drainage. The south-facing slope and the reflected heat from the stone walls let Nebbiolo ripen at latitude 46 N; the Breva wind from Lake Como warms afternoons.
appellations.nerd_note: Working these terraces takes around 1,200 to 1,500 hours per hectare per year, and some grapes are still lowered by cable or helicopter.

appellations.name: Sforzato di Valtellina
match: Sforzato di Valtellina / Sfursat di Valtellina
appellations.summary: Sforzato (in dialect Sfursat, 'forced') is Valtellina's answer to Amarone: Nebbiolo grapes picked in October and dried in airy lofts (*fruttai*) until at least December or January, losing around 30 to 40% of their weight, then fermented dry. The result is a powerful red of 14 to 16% alcohol with dried cherry, fig, tar and spice, but still with Nebbiolo's acidity and tannin. It ages at least 20 months (12 in wood). Nino Negri's 5 Stelle Sfursat, first made by Casimiro Maule in the 1980s, made the category famous.
appellations.terroir: Grapes come from the best terraces of the Valtellina Superiore subzones; the drying lofts use the cold, dry Alpine air.
appellations.nerd_note: Sforzato was the first dried-grape dry red to win DOCG status in Italy (2003), six years ahead of Amarone (2009).

appellations.name: Rosso di Valtellina
appellations.summary: The entry-level Valtellina Nebbiolo, with six months' minimum ageing; bright, light and alpine.
appellations.terroir: Terraced granite and schist slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Arpepe's Rosso di Valtellina is a cult value pick.

appellations.name: Oltrepò Pavese metodo classico
appellations.grapes: Pinot Nero (min 70%), Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio
appellations.summary: Oltrepò Pavese has more Pinot Noir than anywhere else in Italy, about 3,000 hectares, and for a century it supplied base wine to the sparkling houses of Piedmont and beyond. Its own metodo classico DOCG requires at least 70% Pinot Nero and 15 months on the lees (24 for vintage), and the 'Cruasé' brand denotes Pinot Nero rosé. The zone around Santa Maria della Versa, Montalto and Rocca de' Giorgi grows its best sparkling grapes. Conte Vistarino, Monsupello, Ballabio, Calatroni and Mazzolino lead.
appellations.terroir: Clay, limestone and marl hills of the northern Apennines, 150 to 500 m, cooler in the upper valleys (Versa, Scuropasso).
appellations.nerd_note: The Giorgi di Vistarino counts planted Pinot Noir cuttings from France at Rocca de' Giorgi in the 1850s and supplied grapes for some of the first Italian sparkling wines made with Carlo Gancia.

appellations.name: Oltrepò Pavese
appellations.grapes: Barbera, Croatina, Uva Rara, Pinot Nero, Riesling, Moscato and others
appellations.summary: The 'beyond the Po' hills of Pavia province, Lombardy's largest wine zone with about 13,500 hectares, form a triangle wedged between Piedmont and Emilia. The umbrella DOC covers Rosso, Barbera, Riesling (Italian Riesling and Rhine Riesling), Moscato and more. Historically this was Milan's wine cellar, much of it sold in bulk or as sparkling base.
appellations.terroir: Apennine foothills of marl, clay and limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: For decades Oltrepò Pinot Noir went anonymously into the sparkling wines of big Piedmontese houses, which is why the zone's own name is still little known abroad.

appellations.name: Pinot nero dell'Oltrepò Pavese
appellations.summary: Still Pinot Noir from the Oltrepò, red or vinified as white or rosé. Tenuta Mazzolino's Noir and Conte Vistarino's Pernice single vineyard show its Burgundian ambitions.
appellations.terroir: Cool upper valleys of the Oltrepò.
appellations.nerd_note: Frecciarossa's Giorgio Odero bottled Pinot Nero in the 1930s.

appellations.name: Oltrepò Pavese Pinot grigio
appellations.summary: A separate DOC for Pinot Grigio in the Oltrepò hills.

appellations.name: Bonarda dell'Oltrepò Pavese
appellations.summary: The Oltrepò's signature everyday red, usually lightly sparkling (frizzante), purple-black, juicy and gently tannic: made from Croatina, which locals call Bonarda (not to be confused with Piedmont's Bonarda grape). It is the classic match for salame di Varzi and Lombard cooking.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone hills.
appellations.nerd_note: Croatina's local name Bonarda leads to endless confusion with the Bonarda Piemontese grape and Argentina's Bonarda (Douce Noir).

appellations.name: Buttafuoco dell'Oltrepò Pavese
appellations.grapes: Barbera, Croatina, Uva Rara, Ughetta di Canneto
appellations.summary: 'Spark of fire': a powerful red blend from seven communes around Canneto Pavese and Broni. The Buttafuoco Storico association bottles single-vineyard versions with long ageing.
appellations.terroir: Steep hills between the Versa and Scuropasso streams.
appellations.nerd_note: The name is said to come from Austrian sailors on the Po who were 'set on fire' by the wine.

appellations.name: Sangue di Giuda
match: Sangue di Giuda / Sangue di Giuda dell'Oltrepò Pavese
appellations.summary: 'Blood of Judas': a sweet, lightly sparkling red from the same area as Buttafuoco, low in alcohol and drunk with desserts.
appellations.terroir: Hills around Broni and Canneto.
appellations.nerd_note: Legend says Judas, resurrected in the Oltrepò, cured the vines of disease and the wine was named for him.

appellations.name: Casteggio
appellations.summary: A small DOC for structured Barbera from the hills around Casteggio, the Roman Clastidium.
appellations.nerd_note: Clastidium was the site of a famous Roman victory over the Gauls in 222 BC.

appellations.name: Lugana
appellations.summary: Lugana is the white wine of the southern shore of Lake Garda, straddling Lombardy (Sirmione, Desenzano, Pozzolengo, Lonato) and Veneto (Peschiera). It is made from Turbiana, a local grape related to Verdicchio (and once called Trebbiano di Lugana), and grown on heavy, chalky white-grey clays left by the Garda glacier. The wines have citrus, almond and saline depth and age surprisingly well; Superiore, Riserva, Vendemmia Tardiva and Spumante versions exist. Lugana has been one of Italy's commercial success stories of the 2010s and 2020s, with plantings expanding fast.
appellations.terroir: Compact white and grey calcareous clays (marl-clay) from the morainic amphitheatre south of the lake; the lake moderates frosts and summer heat.
appellations.nerd_note: Ca' dei Frati's Brolettino and I Frati, and Ottella's Molceo, showed in the 1980s and 1990s that Lugana could age ten years.

appellations.name: San Martino della Battaglia
appellations.summary: A tiny DOC south of Lake Garda for Friulano, here called Tuchì, dry or as a liqueur wine. It overlaps Lugana's zone around the Risorgimento battlefield of San Martino (1859).
appellations.terroir: Morainic clays.
appellations.nerd_note: The battle of Solferino and San Martino in 1859 inspired Henry Dunant to found the Red Cross.

appellations.name: Riviera del Garda Classico
match: Riviera del Garda Bresciano / Garda Bresciano
appellations.summary: The DOC of the western shore of Lake Garda in Brescia province (formerly Garda Bresciano), for Groppello reds and Chiaretto.
appellations.terroir: Moraine and limestone on the lake's western shore.
appellations.nerd_note: The DOC was formerly Riviera del Garda Bresciano / Garda Bresciano.

appellations.name: Valtènesi
appellations.summary: The hills between Desenzano and Salò on Garda's western shore, the home of Groppello and of Valtènesi Chiaretto, a pale, delicate rosé that Pompeo Molmenti, a Venetian senator, made famous from his estate at Moniga in 1896. It has become one of Italy's most fashionable rosés.
appellations.terroir: Morainic hills with lake breezes.
appellations.nerd_note: Molmenti's 1896 Chiaretto is often cited as the first modern Italian rosé, made by short skin contact in the manner of the Bordeaux clairet.

appellations.name: Garda Colli Mantovani
appellations.grapes: Garganega, Trebbiano, Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet, Rondinella
appellations.summary: Morainic hills south of Lake Garda in Mantua province, making light whites, reds and Chiaretto.
appellations.terroir: Moraine.

appellations.name: Lambrusco Mantovano
appellations.grapes: Lambrusco Viadanese, Maestri, Marani, Salamino, Ruberti
appellations.summary: Lombardy's own Lambrusco from the flat lands of Mantua province south of the Po, lightly sparkling and dry or off-dry, with subzones Viadanese-Sabbionetano and Oltre Po Mantovano.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial plain of the Po.
appellations.nerd_note: Lambrusco Viadanese is a local Lambrusco variety found almost only here.

appellations.name: Botticino
appellations.summary: A small red DOC on the hills east of Brescia, in the village famous for its marble (Botticino marble was used for Rome's Vittoriano monument). The blend of Barbera, Marzemino, Sangiovese and Schiava gives fresh, medium reds.
appellations.terroir: Limestone slopes beside the marble quarries.
appellations.nerd_note: The Vittoriano 'wedding cake' in Rome is built of Botticino marble from the same hills.

appellations.name: Cellatica
appellations.grapes: Marzemino, Barbera, Schiava gentile, Incrocio Terzi
appellations.summary: Tiny red DOC in the hills north-west of Brescia, one of Lombardy's oldest delimited wines.
appellations.terroir: Hills above Brescia.
appellations.nerd_note: Incrocio Terzi No. 1, a Barbera x Cabernet Franc cross, was bred in Brescia province.

appellations.name: Capriano del Colle
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Marzemino, Barbera; Trebbiano (Trebbiano di Lugana)
appellations.summary: Small DOC on Monte Netto, an isolated hill south-west of Brescia.
appellations.terroir: An isolated loess and gravel hill rising from the plain.

appellations.name: Valcalepio
appellations.grapes: Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon (red); Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio (white); Moscato di Scanzo (passito)
appellations.summary: Bergamo's main DOC, on the foothills between Lake Iseo and Bergamo, making Bordeaux-blend reds aged at least two years and a Moscato Passito.
appellations.terroir: Calcareous marls of the Bergamo pre-Alps.

appellations.name: Moscato di Scanzo
appellations.summary: Italy's smallest DOCG, about 31 hectares in the single commune of Scanzorosciate near Bergamo. Moscato di Scanzo is a red Muscat whose grapes are dried for at least 21 days, giving an aromatic sweet red with rose, sage, cherry jam and spice, aged at least two years. Local tradition holds that it was shipped to London and the Russian court in the 18th and 19th centuries and fetched prices to rival the finest wines.
appellations.terroir: Sass del Luna, a local friable marly limestone, on south-facing hills at 250 to 500 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Moscato di Scanzo is a distinct red Muscat variety found only here; it is not Moscato Rosa or Moscato Nero.

appellations.name: Terre del Colleoni
appellations.grapes: Schiava, Marzemino, Incrocio Manzoni, Franconia, Merlot, Cabernet
appellations.summary: Named after the condottiero Bartolomeo Colleoni, this Bergamo DOC covers the hills around Bergamo with a range of varietals including Franconia (Blaufränkisch).

appellations.name: San Colombano al Lambro
match: San Colombano al Lambro / San Colombano
appellations.grapes: Croatina, Barbera, Uva Rara; Chardonnay, Pinot Nero
appellations.summary: The only DOC in Milan's metropolitan province, on an isolated hill rising above the Po plain near Lodi. Light reds of Croatina and Barbera.
appellations.terroir: An isolated hill of marine sediments and loess in the flat plain.
appellations.nerd_note: The hill is named after the Irish monk Saint Columbanus, who passed by on his way to found the abbey of Bobbio in 614.

appellations.name: Alto Adige
match: Alto Adige / dell'Alto Adige / Südtirol / Südtiroler
appellations.grapes: Schiava, Lagrein, Pinot Nero, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Gewürztraminer, Müller-Thurgau, Sylvaner, Kerner, Riesling, Moscato Giallo, Moscato Rosa and others
appellations.summary:
The Alto Adige / Südtirol DOC covers almost all the vineyards of the province of Bolzano, about 5,800 hectares, and is one of the few Italian denominations where whites outnumber reds (around 60% white). It is a varietal-led DOC with a large cast of grapes, unusually high average quality and a dominant cooperative sector that produces many of its top wines.

The DOC was created in 1975 (its 50th anniversary was celebrated at Vinitaly 2025), and it contains subzones that can appear on the label: Santa Maddalena (St. Magdalener) and Colli di Bolzano (Bozner Leiten) around Bolzano, Terlano (Terlaner), Meranese (Meraner), Valle Isarco (Eisacktaler) with its Bressanone (Brixner) and Klausen sections, Val Venosta (Vinschgau) and Lago di Caldaro classico. Since 2024 the DOC also has 86 UGAs, small named areas each with up to five permitted varieties and yields 25% lower than the DOC; a UGA symbol on the label marks these wines, which covered about 403 hectares and 6.7% of DOC production in 2025.

The white benchmarks are Terlano's long-lived Pinot Bianco and Sauvignon (some vintages released after decades on the lees), Tramin's Gewürztraminer Nussbaumer and Epokale, and San Michele Appiano's Sanct Valentin range. Lagrein, a dark native red, is grown on the hot gravels of Gries in Bolzano; Pinot Noir is at its best on the Mazon plateau above Egna and in Appiano Monte (Eppan Berg).
appellations.terroir: Vineyards climb from about 200 m on the Adige valley floor to over 1,000 m in Val Venosta and Valle Isarco. Porphyry around Bolzano and Terlano gives mineral, long-lived wines; dolomitic limestone and moraine in the Bassa Atesina (Termeno, Cortaccia, Magrè) suit Gewürztraminer and Pinot Noir; schist, quartz-phyllite and moraine in the Isarco valley give taut Sylvaner, Kerner and Riesling. Summer heat in the valley bottom contrasts with cool nights from the mountains.
appellations.nerd_note: The 86 UGAs were drawn using, among other evidence, place names from the Theresian Cadastre of the 1770s; Gries, Mazon, Eppan Berg and Brenntal are among the best known.

appellations.name: Santa Maddalena
appellations.summary: The hillside vineyards around the little church of St. Magdalena on the north-eastern edge of Bolzano make Alto Adige's classic Schiava: pale ruby, fragrant with violets, almond and cherry, a touch of Lagrein for colour. Local lore holds that in the 1930s it was ranked among Italy's three great reds, alongside Barolo and Barbaresco. The Classico core is on the steep slopes of Rencio and St. Magdalena.
appellations.terroir: Morainic and porphyry slopes rising behind Bolzano, very warm and sunny.
appellations.nerd_note: The UGAs inside the classico area include St. Justina, Leitach, Rentsch and Prazöll, all small hillside hamlets of Bolzano.

appellations.name: Terlano
appellations.grapes: Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Pinot Grigio, Riesling, Müller-Thurgau
appellations.summary: Terlano is the most famous white-wine village of Alto Adige, between Bolzano and Merano. Its cooperative, the Cantina Terlano (1893), holds back wines for 10 to 30 years before release, proving that Pinot Bianco and Sauvignon from porphyry soils can age like great Burgundy. Terlaner Classico comes from the steep porphyry slopes above the village.
appellations.terroir: Red quartz porphyry, sandy and mineral, on south-facing slopes up to about 900 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Cantina Terlano's 'Rarity' series releases wines that have spent more than a decade on fine lees in steel tanks.

appellations.name: Valle Isarco
appellations.grapes: Sylvaner, Kerner, Müller-Thurgau, Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Grigio, Zweigelt
appellations.summary: The Isarco (Eisack) valley north of Bolzano toward Bressanone and the Brenner Pass is Italy's northernmost wine zone, a land of steep terraces, monasteries and crisp, aromatic whites. Kerner, Sylvaner and Grüner Veltliner are specialities; Bressanone (Brixner) and Klausen are sub-areas. The Abbazia di Novacella (founded 1142) and the Cantina Valle Isarco co-op dominate, with growers like Kuenhof (Peter Pliger), Manni Nössing and Köfererhof.
appellations.terroir: Schist, quartz-phyllite and glacial moraine at 500 to 900 m; cool, with strong day-night swings.
appellations.nerd_note: Kerner, a Schiava x Riesling cross bred in Württemberg in 1929, found its best home in Italy here.

appellations.name: Val Venosta
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Nero, Müller-Thurgau, Kerner, Gewürztraminer
appellations.summary: The dry, high Vinschgau west of Merano, famous for apples, has a small number of vineyards at 500 to 900 m that make taut Riesling and Pinot Noir. Castel Juval, owned by the mountaineer Reinhold Messner, and Falkenstein (Franz Pratzner) are its best-known estates.
appellations.terroir: Gneiss and schist on the sunny northern side of a rain-shadow valley with very low rainfall.
appellations.nerd_note: Reinhold Messner, the first man to climb all 14 eight-thousanders, owns Castel Juval and its vineyard.

appellations.name: Meranese
appellations.summary: Light Schiava from the hills around Merano, the old Habsburg spa town, including the Burgraviato area. Fresh, fruity and meant for drinking young.
appellations.terroir: Moraine and gneiss slopes of the Merano basin.
appellations.nerd_note: Meranese is also called Meraner Hügel (Merano hill) on older labels.

appellations.name: Colli di Bolzano
appellations.summary: Schiava from the slopes around Bolzano outside the St. Magdalener zone, slightly lighter in style.
appellations.terroir: Porphyry and moraine around the Bolzano basin.

appellations.name: Lago di Caldaro
match: Lago di Caldaro / Kalterersee / Caldaro / Kalterer
appellations.summary: Kalterersee, a light, soft Schiava from around Lake Caldaro (Kaltern) south of Bolzano, was once the most exported Italian red to Austria, Germany and Switzerland, drunk by the litre. The DOC is unusual in crossing the provincial border into Trentino. The Classico zone around the lake itself, often labelled Kalterersee Auslese with higher ripeness, has seen a quality revival led by Kellerei Kaltern and Manincor.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and moraine slopes around the warm basin of Lake Caldaro.
appellations.nerd_note: Lake Caldaro is the warmest lake in the Alps, and its microclimate also ripens Cabernet and Merlot on the shores.

appellations.name: Trento
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Nero, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Meunier
appellations.summary:
Trento DOC was Italy's first DOC dedicated to metodo classico sparkling wine (1993) and is the second most important Italian traditional-method appellation after Franciacorta. Vineyards on the slopes of the Adige valley and its side valleys, often at 300 to 800 m, give Chardonnay with high acidity and a mountain freshness. Rules require at least 15 months on the lees (24 for millesimato, 36 for Riserva). The brand 'TrentoDOC' groups about 60 houses.

Giulio Ferrari, who studied in Montpellier and Geisenheim and worked in Champagne, founded his company in 1902 and planted Chardonnay in Trentino; in 1952 he sold it to Bruno Lunelli, whose family built Ferrari into Italy's leading sparkling-wine brand. Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore is one of Italy's great wines. Rotari (Mezzacorona), Cesarini Sforza, Letrari, Revì, Maso Martis, Abate Nero and Altemasi (Cavit) are other names.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, dolomite and porphyry slopes on the hills around Trento, the Valle di Cembra, Valsugana and Vallagarina; mountain altitude preserves acidity.
appellations.nerd_note: Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore comes from the Lunelli family's Maso Pianizza Chardonnay vineyard at around 550 to 600 m and spends about a decade on the lees.

appellations.name: Trentino
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio, Müller-Thurgau, Nosiola, Marzemino, Teroldego, Lagrein, Merlot, Cabernet and many others
appellations.summary: The umbrella DOC for the province of Trento, mostly varietal wines from the Adige valley, the Valle dei Laghi and Vallagarina. Most volume comes from big cooperatives (Cavit, Mezzacorona, La-Vis). Its gems include Marzemino from Isera (the wine Don Giovanni orders in Mozart's opera), Nosiola, the native white, and Vino Santo Trentino, a rare sweet wine from Nosiola grapes dried until Holy Week in the Valle dei Laghi, aged for several years before release.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial valley floors and limestone, porphyry and moraine slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Trentino's Vino Santo grapes are dried on racks (*arele*) until Easter week, and the wine spends years in small casks before release.

appellations.name: Teroldego Rotaliano
appellations.summary:
Teroldego is the 'prince of Trentino', a dark, juicy red grown almost exclusively on the Campo Rotaliano, a triangular gravel plain where the Noce river meets the Adige between Mezzolombardo, Mezzocorona and San Michele all'Adige. It is deep purple, with blackberry, violet and tar, and lively acidity.

Its modern reputation is the work of Elisabetta Foradori, who took over her family estate in Mezzolombardo in 1984, spent years selecting old clones from the vineyards to restore diversity lost to productive modern clones, converted to biodynamics in the 2000s and now ferments single-vineyard Teroldegos (Sgarzon, Morei) in clay amphorae from Spain. DNA work in the 2000s showed that Lagrein is probably Teroldego's offspring, that Marzemino belongs to the same family, and that Teroldego is closely related to Dureza, one of Syrah's parents.
appellations.terroir: Deep alluvial gravels and sands of the Noce fan, well-drained, warm, sheltered by mountain walls on three sides.
appellations.nerd_note: Through its close kinship with Dureza, a parent of Syrah, Teroldego is a distant Alpine cousin of the great Rhône grape.

appellations.name: Casteller
appellations.grapes: Schiava, Merlot, Lambrusco a foglia frastagliata (Enantio) and others
appellations.summary: A light red blend from the hills of Trento and Vallagarina, named after the Casteller hill above Trento.

appellations.name: Valdadige
appellations.grapes: Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay, Schiava, Enantio, Merlot and others
appellations.summary: A cross-regional DOC (Etschtaler in German) running down the Adige valley from Alto Adige through Trentino into the province of Verona, used mostly for Pinot Grigio and light reds.
appellations.terroir: Valley floor alluvium and lower slopes of the Adige.
appellations.nerd_note: One of the few Italian DOCs spanning two regions and three provinces.

appellations.name: Amarone della Valpolicella
appellations.grapes: Corvina and Corvinone (45 to 95%), Rondinella (5 to 30%), plus up to 25% other local reds such as Molinara and Oseleta
appellations.summary:
Amarone is one of the world's most distinctive red wines: dry, powerful (often 15 to 16.5% alcohol) and opulent, made from grapes that have spent three to four months drying (*appassimento*) in airy lofts called *fruttai* until they have lost 30 to 45% of their weight. The concentrated sugars ferment fully dry, giving flavours of dried cherry, fig, chocolate, tobacco and spice with a bitter twist on the finish (*amaro* means bitter, and Amarone means 'big bitter').

It was born almost by accident. Valpolicella's traditional dried-grape wine was the sweet Recioto, and Amarone was originally a Recioto that had fermented all the way to dryness, a fault. The name is said to have been coined in 1936 by Adelino Lucchese, cellar master at the Cantina Sociale Valpolicella, when he tasted such a cask, and Bolla, Bertani and others began selling it commercially in the 1950s. It became a DOC within Recioto della Valpolicella in 1968, a separate DOC in 1990 and a DOCG in 2010 (approved December 2009).

The production zone covers 19 communes and 8,614 hectares of Valpolicella vineyard (2025). In 2025 about 13.6 million bottles of Amarone and Recioto were released, with 327,545 quintals of grapes set aside for drying. Ageing is at least two years from 1 January after harvest (Riserva four), and minimum alcohol is 14%. Giuseppe Quintarelli and Romano Dal Forno make the most sought-after, long-aged versions; Bertani's Classico, released after years in large casks, is the benchmark of the traditional style.
appellations.terroir: Valpolicella is a fan of north-south valleys running down from the Lessini Mountains to the Adige: in the Classico zone the Fumane, Marano and Negrar valleys, then Valpantena, then the eastern valleys of Illasi and Mezzane. Soils are limestone, marl and clay on the hills (red clays on the *marogne*, dry-stone terraces), with volcanic basalt in the east. Higher hillside sites at 300 to 500 m give fresher, more aromatic grapes, while the drying process itself, regulated by humidity and airflow in the fruttai, shapes the wine as much as the vineyard.
appellations.nerd_note: Before drying became mechanised in some cellars, grapes were dried on bamboo racks (*arele*) or hung from rafters; Quintarelli still dries on racks in his attic, and the consortium has proposed the ritual of 'grape-resting' for UNESCO intangible heritage.

appellations.name: Recioto della Valpolicella
appellations.summary: The original dried-grape wine of Valpolicella: sweet, red, rich in cherry and chocolate, made from dried grapes whose fermentation is stopped while sugar remains. It is the direct descendant of the *Acinatico* praised by Cassiodorus around AD 500. The name comes from *recie*, dialect for the 'ears' or upper lobes of the bunch that got the most sun and were selected for drying. Today Recioto is a rarity, a fraction of Amarone's volume, but Quintarelli, Dal Forno and Bussola make thrilling ones.
appellations.terroir: Same hillsides as Amarone.
appellations.nerd_note: Recioto Spumante, a sweet sparkling red, is still permitted and occasionally made.

appellations.name: Valpolicella
appellations.grapes: Corvina and Corvinone (45 to 95%), Rondinella (5 to 30%), others up to 25%
appellations.summary: The everyday red of Verona: light to medium-bodied, with sour cherry, almond and herbs, made from fresh (undried) grapes. Valpolicella Classico comes from the historic heart (Fumane, Marano, Negrar, San Pietro in Cariano, Sant'Ambrogio), Valpantena from the valley north of Verona, and the eastern zone extends to Illasi and Mezzane. Superiore requires a year of ageing. In 2025, 16.5 million bottles of Valpolicella DOC were released. The best (Quintarelli, Bussola, Monte dei Ragni) show that unadorned Corvina can be as compelling as Amarone.
appellations.terroir: Hills of limestone, marl and basalt; the Classico zone sits on limestone, the east more volcanic.
appellations.nerd_note: The name may come from Latin *vallis polis cellae*, 'valley of many cellars', or from the Greek-Latin for 'valley of many'; scholars disagree.

appellations.name: Valpolicella Ripasso
appellations.summary: Ripasso ('re-passed') is Valpolicella refermented on the pomace of Amarone or Recioto, picking up extra alcohol, body, glycerol and dried-fruit flavours. It was popularised by Masi, whose Campofiorin (1964) made the technique famous, and it became its own DOC in 2010. Ripasso is now the biggest seller of the Valpolicella family: 27.4 million bottles in 2025, nearly half the total. Styles range from simple and sweetish to serious, age-worthy wines.
appellations.terroir: Same vineyards as Valpolicella.
appellations.nerd_note: Masi markets Campofiorin as 'IGT Rosso del Veronese' rather than Ripasso, partly because it uses a modified double-fermentation method with dried grapes.

appellations.name: Soave
appellations.grapes: Garganega (min 70%), Trebbiano di Soave and Chardonnay
appellations.summary:
Soave is one of Italy's great white wines and, after its 1970s and 1980s reputation as a cheap supermarket staple, one of its great comeback stories. It is made mainly from Garganega, a late-ripening, thick-skinned grape that gives almond, chamomile, yellow plum and a saline, smoky mineral finish, especially from the volcanic hills. The DOC covers about 7,000 hectares east of Verona, but the heart is Soave Classico, the hills around the medieval walled town of Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone.

In 2019 the consortium mapped 33 UGAs (Unità Geografiche Aggiuntive), covering about 2,660 hectares (38% of the area): 28 in the Classico zone, three in the limestone west (Broia, Paradiso, Monte di Colognola) and two volcanic sites in the east (Duello, Roncà-Monte Calvarina). The names, which can appear on labels from the 2019 vintage, include Foscarino, Froscà, Castelcerino, Fittà, Monte Grande, Pressoni, Carbonare, Volpare and Costalunga. Pieropan (Calvarino, La Rocca), Anselmi, Inama, Gini, Prà, Coffele, Suavia, Filippi and Cantina di Soave are key producers. The Soave hills were also recognised in 2018 by the FAO as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System for their traditional pergola training.
appellations.terroir: Two very different soils meet in the Classico zone. East of the Alpone and on the Monte Foscarino and Castelcerino ridges are dark volcanic basalts and tuffs from Eocene eruptions, giving smoky, saline, structured wines; west, toward Soave and Colognola, are white limestones (Calvarino, La Rocca) giving finer, more floral wines. The vines are traditionally trained on the Veronese pergola, which shades the grapes from summer heat.
appellations.nerd_note: Roberto Anselmi left the DOC in 2000 in protest at its rules and now sells his famous Capitel Foscarino and I Capitelli as IGT Veneto.

appellations.name: Soave Superiore
appellations.summary: The DOCG tier of Soave, with lower yields and longer ageing (Riserva a year). In practice most top producers bottle their best wines as Soave Classico DOC rather than Superiore, so the DOCG remains marginal.
appellations.terroir: Hill vineyards only.
appellations.nerd_note: One of the few cases in Italy where the DOCG is less prestigious in practice than the DOC beneath it.

appellations.name: Recioto di Soave
appellations.summary: Italy's first DOCG for a white sweet wine (1998), from Garganega grapes dried on racks until spring, giving a golden, apricot and almond-scented wine with bright acidity. A sparkling version also exists.
appellations.terroir: Same volcanic and limestone hills as Soave Classico.
appellations.nerd_note: Recioto di Soave was a favourite of the Venetian court and the papal households in the 18th century.

appellations.name: Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco
match: Conegliano Valdobbiadene - Prosecco / Valdobbiadene - Prosecco / Conegliano - Prosecco
appellations.grapes: Glera (min 85%), Verdiso, Bianchetta Trevigiana, Perera, Glera lunga
appellations.summary:
The steep hills between Conegliano and Valdobbiadene in the province of Treviso are the historic heart of Prosecco and its top tier: Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore DOCG. Fifteen communes on a ribbon of ridges at 100 to 500 m, many slopes so steep (the *ciglioni*, grassy terraces) that everything is done by hand, about 600 hours per hectare a year. The landscape became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019.

Prosecco is made mostly by the Martinotti (tank or charmat) method, a second fermentation in pressurised tanks that preserves Glera's fresh pear, apple, wisteria and acacia aromas. Styles range from Extra Brut to Brut, Extra Dry (the traditional and most popular) and Dry, plus Sui Lieviti, the old *col fondo* style refermented in bottle and left cloudy on its lees. The 43 Rive are single-commune or single-hamlet wines from steep slopes with lower yields (13 tonnes/ha) and a vintage on the label; at the summit is Superiore di Cartizze, 107 hectares of steep hills in San Pietro di Barbozza, Santo Stefano and Saccol in Valdobbiadene, traditionally made Dry.

The Scuola Enologica in Conegliano, founded in 1876, and the sparkling wines of Antonio Carpenè, who founded his house in 1868, laid the foundations; Nino Franco, Bisol, Adami, Ruggeri, Bortolomiol, Col Vetoraz and Villa Sandi are leading houses.
appellations.terroir: Marine and glacial conglomerates, sandstones and marls folded into steep east-west hogbacks; the Pre-Alps shelter the hills from cold winds, and the Piave river and Adriatic breezes temper summer heat. Valdobbiadene, to the west, is higher, steeper and cooler; Conegliano, to the east, is gentler and warmer.
appellations.nerd_note: Cartizze vineyard land is among the most expensive in Italy, regularly quoted at well over a million euros per hectare, on a par with top Barolo crus.

appellations.name: Asolo Prosecco
appellations.summary: The second Prosecco Superiore DOCG, on the Asolo and Montello hills west of the Piave around the hill town of Asolo, once home of Caterina Cornaro, Queen of Cyprus. It grew rapidly in the 2010s and is known for pioneering the drier Extra Brut style and allowing Brut Nature.
appellations.terroir: Gentler, sunnier slopes of sandy marl and limestone around Asolo and on the Montello.
appellations.nerd_note: Asolo was one of the first Prosecco zones to embrace bone-dry Extra Brut.

appellations.name: Prosecco
appellations.grapes: Glera (min 85%); Pinot Nero (10 to 15%) for rosé
appellations.summary:
The Prosecco DOC is the world's best-selling sparkling wine and Italy's largest wine appellation by value. Created in 2009, it spans nine provinces in Veneto (Treviso, Venezia, Vicenza, Padova, Belluno) and Friuli Venezia Giulia (Trieste, Gorizia, Udine, Pordenone), a defensive move: the grape was renamed Glera and the name Prosecco, taken from the village of Prosecco near Trieste, became a protected place name that no one outside the zone could use.

Production reached 667 million bottles in 2025 (607 million white and 60 million rosé, a category introduced in 2020), with the United States the largest export market. The vineyard potential of about 24,450 hectares is being raised by 6,050 hectares to 30,500, in two phases approved by both regions in late 2025. Treviso and Trieste provinces may add their names to the label ('Prosecco DOC Treviso', 'Prosecco DOC Trieste').
appellations.terroir: Mostly flat alluvial plains of the Piave, Livenza and Tagliamento, with fertile gravels and clays allowing high yields (18 tonnes/ha).
appellations.nerd_note: The village of Prosecco that gave its name to the wine is a suburb of Trieste in Friuli, not in the Treviso hills where the wine is most associated.

appellations.name: Bardolino
appellations.grapes: Corvina (35 to 95%), Rondinella (5 to 40%), Molinara and others
appellations.summary: Bardolino is the light, fragrant red of Lake Garda's eastern shore: pale, cherry-and-spice scented, the sort of red you chill slightly and drink with lake fish. Bardolino Chiaretto, its pink sibling, is one of Italy's most popular rosés and has been reinvented since 2014 as a pale, Provence-style wine. Three subzones, La Rocca, Montebaldo and Sommacampagna, were added in the early 2020s to recognise different soils and exposures.
appellations.terroir: Glacial moraine hills around the lake; the lake moderates temperatures.
appellations.nerd_note: The Bardolino Chiaretto 'Rosé Revolution' of 2014 reduced skin contact to give a paler, lighter wine, reversing decades of darker rosé.

appellations.name: Bardolino Superiore
appellations.summary: The DOCG tier of Bardolino with lower yields and a year of ageing; a small category.
appellations.terroir: Moraine hills east of Garda.

appellations.name: Custoza
appellations.grapes: Garganega, Trebbiano Toscano, Bianca Fernanda (Cortese), Friulano, Malvasia, Riesling, Chardonnay, Manzoni
appellations.summary: Bianco di Custoza is a light, aromatic white blend from the moraine hills south-east of Lake Garda, between Verona and Peschiera. Fresh, floral and slightly almondy; Monte del Frà, Cavalchina and Gorgo are leading names.
appellations.terroir: Glacial moraine of the Garda amphitheatre.
appellations.nerd_note: Custoza was the site of two battles of the Risorgimento (1848 and 1866), and a war ossuary stands among the vineyards.

appellations.name: Gambellara
appellations.summary: Soave's volcanic neighbour across the provincial border in Vicenza, making Garganega whites on dark basalt; Angiolino Maule's La Biancara made it a natural-wine reference. Recioto di Gambellara (DOCG) and Vin Santo di Gambellara are its sweet wines.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic basalt hills.

appellations.name: Recioto di Gambellara
appellations.summary: Sweet dried-grape Garganega from the Gambellara hills, still or sparkling.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic hills.

appellations.name: Lessini Durello
appellations.summary: Durella is a fiercely acidic white grape from the volcanic Lessini hills north of Soave, perfect for sparkling wine. Lessini Durello is made by tank or traditional method; the long-aged Monti Lessini metodo classico versions (36+ months on lees) are among Italy's most underrated sparklers.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic basalts and tuffs of the Alpone and Chiampo valleys up to 600 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Durella's name is thought to come from its tough (*dura*) skin.

appellations.name: Monti Lessini
appellations.grapes: Durella, Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Nero
appellations.summary: Companion DOC to Lessini Durello for still whites and long-aged metodo classico from the Lessini mountains.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic hills.

appellations.name: Breganze
appellations.grapes: Vespaiola, Friulano (Tai), Pinot Bianco, Cabernet, Merlot
appellations.summary: Breganze, on the foothills of the Asiago plateau north of Vicenza, is famous for Torcolato, a golden sweet wine from Vespaiola grapes twisted (*torcolati*) onto strings and hung from rafters to dry until January. Fausto Maculan made Torcolato and his botrytised Acininobili internationally known from the 1980s.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic and morainic soils on south-facing foothills.
appellations.nerd_note: Vespaiola is named after the wasps (*vespe*) attracted to its sweet, ripe grapes.

appellations.name: Colli Euganei
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet, Carmenère, Raboso; Garganega, Pinella, Serprina (Glera), Moscato
appellations.summary: The Euganean Hills south-west of Padua are a cluster of extinct volcanic cones rising from the plain, where Petrarch spent his last years at Arquà. They make Bordeaux-style reds of surprising depth (Vignalta's Gemola, Ca' Lustra) on trachyte and volcanic soils, plus whites from local grapes like Pinella.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic trachyte, rhyolite and latite cones with marine limestone on the lower slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Castello di Lispida in Monselice was one of the first Italian estates to ferment in amphorae, in the 2000s.

appellations.name: Colli Euganei Fior d'Arancio
match: Colli Euganei Fior d'Arancio / Fior d'Arancio Colli Euganei
appellations.summary: 'Orange blossom': Moscato Giallo from the Euganean Hills, made as a sweet sparkling wine, still, or passito. It tastes literally of orange flowers and apricot.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic hills.
appellations.nerd_note: The DOCG is unusual for being dedicated to Moscato Giallo, the yellow Muscat more common in Alto Adige.

appellations.name: Colli Berici
appellations.grapes: Tai Rosso (Grenache), Cabernet, Carmenère, Merlot, Garganega
appellations.summary: Limestone hills south of Vicenza, home of Tai Rosso, a local form of Grenache (Cannonau), especially around Barbarano Vicentino. Inama's Carmenère and Piú show the area's Bordeaux side.
appellations.terroir: Karstic limestone and marl hills with red clays.
appellations.nerd_note: Tai Rosso was called Tocai Rosso until the EU banned the 'Tocai' name in 2007.

appellations.name: Piave
appellations.grapes: Raboso Piave, Merlot, Cabernet, Carmenère, Tai, Verduzzo
appellations.summary: The flat plain along the Piave river in Treviso and Venice provinces, the homeland of Raboso, a tough, high-acid red grape, and of easy Merlot and Cabernet.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial gravels and clays of the Piave plain.
appellations.nerd_note: Raboso is said to take its name from the river Raboso, a tributary of the Piave, or from *rabbioso* ('angry'), describing its acidity.

appellations.name: Piave Malanotte
appellations.summary: A DOCG for Raboso from the Piave, in which 15 to 30% of the grapes are dried before fermentation to tame the grape's fierce acidity and tannin. Aged at least 36 months. Named after the Malanotte borgo at Vazzola.
appellations.terroir: Gravel and clay of the Piave plain.
appellations.nerd_note: Raboso was historically shipped to Venice because its acidity let it survive long sea voyages.

appellations.name: Lison
appellations.summary: A DOCG for Friulano, called Tai here, from the plain on the Veneto-Friuli border around Lison and Portogruaro: floral, almondy whites. Lison Classico is the historic core.
appellations.terroir: Clay and calcareous alluvium ('caranto' hardpan).

appellations.name: Lison-Pramaggiore
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet, Refosco, Malbech, Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay, Verduzzo
appellations.summary: Varietal DOC across the Veneto-Friuli border, with Refosco and Malbech among its curiosities.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial plain.

appellations.name: Montello Rosso
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Carmenère
appellations.summary: A DOCG for Bordeaux-style reds from the Montello hill near Treviso. Loredan Gasparini's Venegazzù della Casa, a Bordeaux blend first made in the 1950s, was one of the earliest Italian Cabernet-based reds of ambition.
appellations.terroir: Red clays over karst on the Montello hill.

appellations.name: Asolo Montello
appellations.summary: Varietal DOC for the Asolo and Montello hills.

appellations.name: Bagnoli Friularo
appellations.summary: Raboso, here called Friularo, from the plain around Bagnoli di Sopra south of Padua, dry or as a passito. The Borletti family's Dominio di Bagnoli, an estate founded on Benedictine lands, is the reference.
appellations.terroir: Clay plain.
appellations.nerd_note: Bagnoli's great estate was a Benedictine property before passing to Venetian nobility, and the Friularo name recalls the grape's reputed Friulian origin.

appellations.name: Bagnoli di Sopra
appellations.summary: Varietal and blended wines from the Bagnoli plain south of Padua.

appellations.name: Arcole
appellations.summary: A plain-land DOC south of Soave, named after Napoleon's 1796 victory at the bridge of Arcole.
appellations.nerd_note: Napoleon's charge across the Arcole bridge is depicted in Antoine-Jean Gros's famous painting.

appellations.name: Colli di Conegliano
appellations.grapes: Cabernet, Merlot, Marzemino; Manzoni Bianco, Pinot Bianco; Verdiso; Torchiato di Fregona
appellations.summary: A small DOCG (since 2011) for still wines from the Prosecco hills: Bordeaux-variety reds and Manzoni Bianco whites, the rare sweet Torchiato di Fregona from dried grapes, and the red Refrontolo Passito from Marzemino.
appellations.nerd_note: Refrontolo's Marzemino passito is said to be the Marzemino Mozart's Don Giovanni toasts.

appellations.name: Corti Benedettine del Padovano
appellations.summary: Plain wines from lands once farmed by Benedictine monasteries south of Padua.
appellations.nerd_note: The name recalls the *corti* (farm courtyards) of the Benedictine abbey of Santa Giustina.

appellations.name: Garda
appellations.grapes: Garganega, Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio, Corvina, Merlot and many others
appellations.summary: A large inter-regional varietal DOC around Lake Garda spanning Veneto and Lombardy.

appellations.name: Merlara
appellations.summary: A small plain DOC on the Adige near the Padua-Verona border.

appellations.name: Riviera del Brenta
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet, Raboso, Pinot Bianco, Tai
appellations.summary: Wines from the Brenta canal country between Padua and Venice, lined with Palladian villas.

appellations.name: Venezia
appellations.grapes: Pinot Grigio, Merlot, Cabernet, Raboso, Manzoni Bianco
appellations.summary: Umbrella DOC for the provinces of Venice and Treviso, used for Pinot Grigio and varietals; includes vineyards on the lagoon islands.
appellations.nerd_note: Venissa's walled vineyard on the island of Mazzorbo revived Dorona, a golden lagoon grape almost lost to floods and abandonment.

appellations.name: Vicenza
appellations.grapes: Garganega, Pinot, Cabernet, Merlot and others
appellations.summary: Umbrella DOC for the province of Vicenza.

appellations.name: Vigneti della Serenissima
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Nero, Pinot Grigio
appellations.summary: A Veneto-wide DOC for metodo classico sparkling wine, named for the Most Serene Republic of Venice.

appellations.name: Valdadige Terradeiforti
appellations.summary: A small DOC in the narrow Adige gorge between Verona and Trento, home of the rare Enantio (Lambrusco a foglia frastagliata) and Casetta reds.
appellations.nerd_note: The 'land of forts' is named for the Austrian fortifications guarding the Adige valley.

appellations.name: delle Venezie
appellations.summary: Created in 2017 (registered in the EU in 2020) to regulate Pinot Grigio from Veneto, Friuli Venezia Giulia and the province of Trento, which together make most of the world's Italian Pinot Grigio. It covers tens of thousands of hectares and is by far the largest Pinot Grigio appellation in the world.
appellations.terroir: Plains and foothills across three regions.
appellations.nerd_note: It is one of the few Italian DOCs that also has a Slovene name, Beneških okolišev, for the Slovene-speaking areas of Friuli.

appellations.name: Collio
appellations.grapes: Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Malvasia Istriana, Pinot Grigio, Pinot Bianco, Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Nero
appellations.summary:
Collio Goriziano, usually just Collio, is a crescent of hills between Gorizia and the Slovenian border, around Cormons, Capriva, San Floriano, Oslavia and Dolegna. With roughly 1,300 to 1,500 hectares it is small, but it has the best claim to be Italy's greatest white-wine zone. Its wines are aromatic yet structured and saline, from Friulano (pear, almond, meadow herbs), Ribolla Gialla (citrus, high acid), Malvasia Istriana, Sauvignon and Pinot Grigio, and especially from the field blend that Collio's growers call Collio Bianco, made from native grapes.

The zone was the cradle of the 1960s white revolution: Mario Schiopetto at Capriva, inspired by German and Alsatian cellars, used stainless steel and cool fermentation to make clean varietal whites; Josko Gravner and Stanko Radikon at Oslavia later went the other way, back to long skin maceration and amphorae. The Collio continues across the border as Goriška Brda in Slovenia, where growers like Movia and Marjan Simčič farm the same hills. The DOC was among the first in Italy (1968) and its consortium has spent the 2020s promoting Collio Bianco, a blend from local grapes, as the zone's signature wine.
appellations.terroir: Ponca: layers of Eocene marl and sandstone that weather into friable, calcareous, mineral soils on terraced slopes of 100 to 300 m. The Julian Alps shelter the hills from the north, the Adriatic is 25 km south, and wide day-night temperature swings sharpen aromatics.
appellations.nerd_note: Edi Keber convinced his neighbours to make a single Collio white blend from native grapes, and his estate now makes essentially only that one wine.

appellations.name: Friuli Colli Orientali
appellations.grapes: Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Sauvignon, Verduzzo, Picolit, Refosco, Schioppettino, Pignolo, Tazzelenghe, Merlot, Cabernet
appellations.summary: The eastern hills of the province of Udine, from Tarcento in the north through Cividale, Prepotto, Corno di Rosazzo and Buttrio to Manzano, continuing the Collio toward the north-west. Larger and more varied than Collio, the Colli Orientali are the home of Friuli's great native reds: Schioppettino (peppery, cool-climate, revived by Paolo Rapuzzi of Ronchi di Cialla in the 1970s), Pignolo (dark, tannic, rescued from the Abbey of Rosazzo's vineyards) and Refosco, as well as some of the finest Friulano and sweet Verduzzo and Picolit. Subzones include Cialla, Prepotto (for Schioppettino), Rosazzo (now a separate DOCG) and Ramandolo (DOCG). Miani, Le Due Terre, Ronchi di Cialla, Bastianich, Ronco del Gnemiz, Dorigo and Livio Felluga are leading names.
appellations.terroir: Ponca flysch on terraced hills, with cooler, wetter conditions toward the north near the Alps.
appellations.nerd_note: Schioppettino's name refers to the 'little shots' or pops of its crisp berries, or to the faint prickle the wine once had; the variety was not even officially authorised until the late 1970s, after the Rapuzzis' campaign.

appellations.name: Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit
appellations.summary: Picolit is one of Italy's rarest and most romantic sweet wines, from a grape whose flowers are largely sterile, so it sets only a few berries per bunch ('picolit' means 'little'). Grapes are dried on the vine or on mats to make a delicate, honeyed wine with apricot and acacia. In the 18th century Count Fabio Asquini of Fagagna sold it to the courts of Europe in hand-blown Murano bottles; it was revived in the 20th century by Giuseppe Perusini of Rocca Bernarda. The Cialla subzone has its own label.
appellations.terroir: Ponca hills of the Colli Orientali.
appellations.nerd_note: Picolit's natural floral abortion (it sets as few as a dozen berries per bunch) keeps yields so low that it was nearly abandoned in the 19th century.

appellations.name: Ramandolo
appellations.summary: Friuli's first DOCG (2001): sweet Verduzzo from the steep, wet hills around Ramandolo and Nimis north of Udine, where the Alps rise abruptly. The grapes are late-harvested or dried; the wine is golden, honeyed and almondy, with a tannic grip unusual in a sweet white. The Dri family (Il Roncat) and Anna Berra are reference producers.
appellations.terroir: Steep ponca terraces at 350 to 500 m in one of the wettest wine zones of Italy, below Monte Bernadia.
appellations.nerd_note: Verduzzo's tannin comes from its thick skins, making Ramandolo one of the few sweet whites with noticeable grip.

appellations.name: Rosazzo
appellations.grapes: Friulano (min 50%), Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Ribolla Gialla
appellations.summary: A DOCG for white blends from the hills around the Abbey of Rosazzo in Manzano, Corno di Rosazzo, Premariacco, San Giovanni al Natisone and Buttrio. Livio Felluga's Terre Alte, first made in 1981, is the archetypal Rosazzo blend. Rosazzo Pignolo, though famous, falls under Colli Orientali rules.
appellations.terroir: Ponca hills around the abbey, well ventilated, with a warm microclimate.
appellations.nerd_note: The Abbey of Rosazzo, founded around 1070, preserved the last Pignolo vines through the 20th century.

appellations.name: Carso
appellations.summary: The Karst plateau that runs from Trieste into Slovenia is a land of limestone, sinkholes, caves and the fierce Bora wind, where small growers carve vineyards out of rock and dig cellars into the stone. Native Vitovska and Malvasia Istriana make saline, mineral whites, often skin-macerated in amphorae; Terrano, a local Refosco, gives a sharp, iron-rich red. Edi Kante, Paolo Vodopivec, Benjamin Zidarich and Sandi Skerk have made the Carso a pilgrimage site for natural-wine lovers.
appellations.terroir: Karst limestone with thin red *terra rossa* soils, often bulldozed and crushed by hand to make vineyards; strong winds and Adriatic influence.
appellations.nerd_note: Pliny wrote that the Empress Livia attributed her 86 years to Pucinum, a wine from the rocky coast near Trieste, often identified with today's Prosecco and Carso area.

appellations.name: Friuli Isonzo
appellations.grapes: Friulano, Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Malvasia, Merlot, Cabernet, Refosco
appellations.summary: The plain along the Isonzo river south of the Collio, from Gradisca to Mariano and Romans, on red, iron-rich gravels. Gianfranco Gallo's Vie di Romans proved that this flat land could make whites as powerful as any in the hills, and Lis Neris and Ronco del Gelso followed.
appellations.terroir: Ferrous red gravels and clays of the Isonzo terraces on the right bank; whiter calcareous gravels on the left.
appellations.nerd_note: Isonzo's 'rive alte' (high banks) and 'rive basse' have different soils, which producers label separately.

appellations.name: Friuli Grave
appellations.grapes: Pinot Grigio, Friulano, Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet, Refosco
appellations.summary: The largest DOC in Friuli, on the vast gravel plain of the Tagliamento and Cellina rivers in Pordenone and Udine provinces. Most of Friuli's volume Pinot Grigio, Merlot and Prosecco base comes from here. The village of Rauscedo hosts the world's largest grapevine nursery cooperative (Vivai Cooperativi Rauscedo), which supplies tens of millions of grafted vines a year worldwide.
appellations.terroir: Deep, stony gravels (*grave*) that drain quickly and heat up, with strong day-night swings near the mountains.
appellations.nerd_note: Rauscedo's nurseries produce a large share of all grafted vines planted in Italy, and many in the world.

appellations.name: Friuli Aquileia
appellations.grapes: Refosco, Merlot, Cabernet, Friulano, Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: The plain around the Roman city of Aquileia toward the lagoon of Grado. Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso is the local specialty. The Basilica of Aquileia, with its fourth-century mosaic floor, is a UNESCO site.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial clays and sands near the lagoon.
appellations.nerd_note: Aquileia was a major wine port in Roman times and amphorae from its trade fill the local museum.

appellations.name: Friuli Latisana
appellations.grapes: Friulano, Pinot Grigio, Refosco, Merlot, Cabernet
appellations.summary: A plain DOC on the lower Tagliamento near the Venetian border, making light varietal wines.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial plain.

appellations.name: Friuli Annia
appellations.summary: A small DOC near the lagoon of Marano, named after the Roman Via Annia that ran from Aquileia to Padua.
appellations.terroir: Clay and sandy soils by the lagoon.

appellations.name: Friuli
match: Friuli / Friuli Venezia Giulia / Furlanija / Furlanija Julijska krajina
appellations.summary: The regional DOC Friuli / Friuli Venezia Giulia (with Friulian and Slovene names Furlanija / Furlanija Julijska krajina), created in 2016 to give the whole region a single, recognisable name for exported varietal wines.
appellations.nerd_note: It is one of the only Italian DOCs with names in four languages: Italian, Friulian and two Slovene forms.

appellations.name: Lambrusco di Sorbara
appellations.summary: The palest, most elegant Lambrusco, from the plain north of Modena around Sorbara and Bomporto between the Secchia and Panaro rivers. Lambrusco di Sorbara has a flower that often fails to set (it needs Salamino nearby as a pollinator), giving small bunches of light-coloured grapes; the wine is coral pink to pale ruby, with violet, strawberry and razor acidity. It is made by tank, by the ancestral method (rifermented in bottle and left cloudy) or by metodo classico. Cleto Chiarli, Paltrinieri (Radice, Leclisse), Cavicchioli (Vigna del Cristo), Vittorio Graziano and Cantina di Sorbara are references.
appellations.terroir: Sandy alluvial soils between two rivers, whose sandiness gives perfume and lightness.
appellations.nerd_note: Sorbara's poor fruit set (*acinellatura*) is why growers interplant Salamino as a pollinator, a rare case of a classic wine grape that needs a partner.

appellations.name: Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro
appellations.summary: The darkest and most tannic Lambrusco, from the foothills south of Modena around Castelvetro, Maranello and Vignola. Grasparossa (named for its stems that turn red in autumn) gives deep purple, foaming wines with blackberry and a dry, slightly bitter finish, perfect with zampone and cotechino.
appellations.terroir: Clay and limestone foothills of the Apennines.
appellations.nerd_note: Castelvetro's medieval checkerboard square inspired the town's Dama Vivente (living chess) festival, held every two years.

appellations.name: Lambrusco Salamino di Santa Croce
appellations.summary: From the plain around Santa Croce near Carpi, Salamino (its cylindrical bunch resembles a small salami) is the most widely planted Lambrusco and gives a balance between Sorbara's fragrance and Grasparossa's body.
appellations.terroir: Clay and silt plain of the Secchia.

appellations.name: Modena
appellations.summary: The umbrella DOC for the province of Modena, used mostly for Lambrusco di Modena blends.
appellations.terroir: Plain and foothills.

appellations.name: Reggiano
appellations.grapes: Lambrusco Salamino, Maestri, Marani, Montericco, Ancellotta
appellations.summary: The Lambrusco of Reggio Emilia, typically darker and softer than Modena's thanks to Ancellotta and the Maestri and Marani varieties; most volume of 'Lambrusco Reggiano' comes from here, including much of the sweet export style. Medici Ermete's single-vineyard Concerto (from Salamino) helped show the zone's potential for dry, serious Lambrusco.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial plain of Reggio Emilia.
appellations.nerd_note: Lini 910 is known for a long-aged metodo classico Lambrusco, a rarity in a zone dominated by the tank method.

appellations.name: Colli di Scandiano e di Canossa
match: Colli di Scandiano e di Canossa
appellations.grapes: Spergola, Malvasia, Sauvignon, Lambrusco Grasparossa, Marzemino
appellations.summary: Hill wines south of Reggio Emilia around the castle of Canossa (where Emperor Henry IV knelt before Pope Gregory VII in 1077), notably Spergola, a high-acid white now made as sparkling and still wine.
appellations.terroir: Clay and marl foothills.
appellations.nerd_note: Spergola was long confused with Sauvignon until DNA showed it is a distinct local grape.

appellations.name: Colli Piacentini
appellations.grapes: Barbera, Croatina (Bonarda), Malvasia di Candia, Ortrugo, Trebbiano, Pinot Nero
appellations.summary: The hills of Piacenza province, continuing the Oltrepò Pavese, form four valleys (Tidone, Trebbia, Nure, Arda). The DOC has subzones Vigoleno (for a rare Vin Santo), Val Trebbia, Val Nure and Val d'Arda. Malvasia di Candia Aromatica makes aromatic whites still, sparkling or passito; La Stoppa's Ageno, a skin-macerated Malvasia blend by Elena Pantaleoni, is one of Italy's most influential orange wines.
appellations.terroir: Clay and marl Apennine foothills.
appellations.nerd_note: Vin Santo di Vigoleno is made in tiny quantities from grapes dried for months in the medieval borgo of Vigoleno.

appellations.name: Gutturnio
appellations.summary: Piacenza's signature red, Barbera blended with Croatina (Bonarda), made still or frizzante; Gutturnio Riserva and Superiore are the serious versions. Named after a Roman silver drinking vessel (*gutturnium*) found near Veleia.
appellations.terroir: Clay and limestone hills of the Val Tidone and Val Nure.
appellations.nerd_note: The Roman silver jug that inspired the name was found at the Roman town of Veleia in the Piacenza hills.

appellations.name: Ortrugo dei Colli Piacentini
match: Ortrugo dei Colli Piacentini / Ortrugo – Colli Piacentini
appellations.summary: Ortrugo, a native white grape (its name means 'other grape'), makes light, almondy sparkling and still wines in the Piacenza hills.
appellations.terroir: Clay foothills.

appellations.name: Colli di Parma
appellations.grapes: Malvasia di Candia Aromatica, Sauvignon, Barbera, Bonarda, Lambrusco
appellations.summary: The hills around Langhirano and Sala Baganza, famous for prosciutto, make Malvasia frizzante and light red sparklers to match.
appellations.terroir: Clay and marl hills.

appellations.name: Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto
appellations.summary: Pignoletto is a crisp, lightly aromatic white from the hills south-west of Bologna, made still, frizzante, spumante and passito; the grape is the same as Umbria's Grechetto Gentile. A broader Pignoletto DOC covers the plain and surrounding provinces, while the hill DOCG is registered as Colli Bolognesi Classico Pignoletto. Orsi San Vito's col fondo and Gaggioli and Manaresi's still wines are references.
appellations.terroir: Clay, sand and limestone hills of the Reno, Lavino and Samoggia valleys.
appellations.nerd_note: Pliny mentioned 'Pino Laeto' wines from the Bologna area, which some link to Pignoletto.

appellations.name: Colli Bolognesi
appellations.grapes: Barbera, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pignoletto, Sauvignon, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: The hills south of Bologna, home to Bordeaux varieties since the 19th century; Enrico Vallania's Terre Rosse estate was an early pioneer of Cabernet in these hills.
appellations.terroir: Clay and sandstone hills.

appellations.name: Romagna Albana
appellations.summary: Albana became Italy's first white DOCG in 1987, a decision widely mocked at the time because most Albana was dull and the promotion looked political. Since then producers have made the case: Albana is a thick-skinned, tannic white grape with apricot, almond and saffron notes, made dry (secco), amabile, sweet (dolce) and above all passito from dried or botrytised grapes. Fattoria Zerbina's Scacco Matto passito and Tre Monti's skin-contact Vitalba helped change minds. The zone covers hills of Bologna, Forlì-Cesena, Ravenna and Rimini provinces, centred on Bertinoro, Dozza and Faenza.
appellations.terroir: Calcareous clays and spungone sandstone of the Romagna foothills.
appellations.nerd_note: Legend says Galla Placidia, daughter of Emperor Theodosius, tasted Albana at Bertinoro and said it should be drunk 'in gold', which supposedly gave the hill town its name.

appellations.name: Romagna
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (min 95% for Romagna Sangiovese), Trebbiano, Cagnina (Refosco), Pagadebit (Bombino Bianco)
appellations.summary: The Romagna DOC unites the region's historic denominations: Romagna Sangiovese (formerly Sangiovese di Romagna, DOC 1967), Romagna Trebbiano, Romagna Cagnina (a sweet red from Refosco, drunk with roast chestnuts in autumn) and Romagna Pagadebit ('pays the debts', a hardy white). Sangiovese is the core: the hills are divided into 12 sottozone (MGAs) that may appear on the label: Serra, Brisighella, Marzeno, Oriolo, Modigliana, Castrocaro, Predappio, Bertinoro, Cesena, San Vicino, Longiano and Meldola. Each has a distinct character: Modigliana on high, cool marl-sandstone at 180 to 570 m gives tense, pale wines; Predappio's red clays give silky tannin; Bertinoro's spungone gives power. Riserva ages two years. Romagna Sangiovese Superiore is the standard bearer; producers include Fattoria Zerbina, Torre San Martino, Villa Papiano, Il Pratello, Fattoria Nicolucci, Noelia Ricci, Tenuta La Viola and Giovanna Madonia.
appellations.terroir: Apennine foothills from Imola to Rimini: spungone, calcareous clays, red clays and marl-sandstone, at 100 to 600 m, with sea breezes from the Adriatic.
appellations.nerd_note: Modigliana's growers formed their own association, Modigliana Stella dell'Appennino, and argue that their cool, high, marl-sandstone valleys make Sangiovese closer to Chianti Classico than to the rest of Romagna.

appellations.name: Colli di Faenza
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet, Merlot, Ciliegiolo, Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay, Trebbiano
appellations.summary: Hill blends around Faenza, the ceramics town.

appellations.name: Colli d'Imola
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet, Barbera, Trebbiano, Pignoletto, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Varietal and blended wines from the Imola hills, home of the Formula One circuit.

appellations.name: Colli di Rimini
appellations.summary: Hill wines behind Rimini, including the sweet Rebola.
appellations.nerd_note: Rebola is a local name for Grechetto Gentile, the same grape as Pignoletto.

appellations.name: Colli Romagna Centrale
appellations.summary: Hill blends from the central Romagna Apennines around Cesena and Forlì.

appellations.name: Bosco Eliceo
appellations.summary: The DOC of the sandy coastal dunes and pine woods of the Po delta near Ferrara and Ravenna, famous for Fortana, an acidic, lightly sparkling red often ungrafted on the sand.
appellations.nerd_note: Fortana grows on its own roots in the delta sands, where phylloxera cannot survive.

appellations.name: Pignoletto
appellations.summary: The broad DOC created in 2014 for Pignoletto from the plain and hills of Bologna, Modena and Ravenna provinces, mostly frizzante and spumante; the hill classic is the Colli Bolognesi Classico Pignoletto DOCG.
appellations.nerd_note: Creating the DOC made Pignoletto a protected place name, so the grape must now be called Grechetto Gentile on labels elsewhere.

appellations.name: Reno
appellations.summary: A plain DOC north of Bologna along the Reno river, known for the local Montuni white grape.

sites.name: Cannubi
sites.text: The most famous name in Barolo and the first to appear on a label: a bottle marked 'Cannubi 1752' is said to survive. The long, low hill runs north-east out of Barolo village, its crest a geological seam where the Tortonian blue marls of La Morra meet the sandier Serravallian layers, which is why Cannubi wines combine perfume and power. The historic core (about 15 ha) faces south-east at 250 to 320 m; the MGA name was disputed in court for years before the core and its four 'Cannubi ...' neighbours were allowed to share it.

sites.name: Cannubi Boschis
sites.text: The north-eastern, east-facing end of the Cannubi hill above the road to Alba. Luciano Sandrone made it famous with his first Barolo, the 1978 Cannubi Boschis, made in a garage while he still worked as cellar master at Marchesi di Barolo; it became one of the defining modernist wines. Since 2013 Sandrone labels it 'Aleste', a play on his grandchildren's names, because the old name was folded into the MGA rules.

sites.name: Cannubi San Lorenzo
sites.text: The southern slope of the Cannubi hill closest to Barolo village. San Lorenzo is also the name of the patron saint chapel area, and with Cannubi, Rué and Rocche it was one of the four vineyards Bartolo Mascarello's father blended into his single Barolo. Giuseppe Rinaldi bottled 'Cannubi San Lorenzo-Ravera' until the MGA rules banned two names on one label, and renamed it Tre Tine.

sites.name: Cannubi Valletta
sites.text: The western flank of the Cannubi hill, facing south-west into the little valley (*valletta*) that separates Cannubi from Sarmassa. Slightly cooler and more sheltered than the core, it gives fragrant, fine-tannined wines.

sites.name: Cannubi Muscatel
sites.text: The south-western tip of the Cannubi hill above the hamlet of Muscatel, named for the Moscato once grown here. It is the smallest and least known of the Cannubi family, on sandier soils near the village.

sites.name: Sarmassa
sites.text: A spur between Brunate and Cannubi on the Barolo side of the La Morra border. Its compact, chalky marls make darker, firmer wines than Cannubi; Marchesi di Barolo and Roberto Voerzio bottle it, and Giacomo Brezza's Sarmassa is a classic of the traditional school.

sites.name: Le Coste
sites.text: Steep, south-facing slopes just south-west of Barolo village on the road toward Vergne. Giuseppe Rinaldi's 'Brunate-Le Coste' blend was split when the MGA rules forbade double names; Le Coste now goes into his Tre Tine and Bussia. Sandy, well-drained soils give a fine, aromatic Barolo.

sites.name: Castellero
sites.text: A small, south-west-facing slope east of Barolo village toward the Castiglione Falletto border. Giacomo Brezza and the Barale family make classic, medium-weight Castellero from old vines.

sites.name: Terlo
sites.text: South-east of Barolo village toward Monforte and Novello, bordering Ravera. Higher and cooler than Cannubi, it gives tight, mineral wines that have gained favour in warm vintages.

sites.name: Paiagallo
