sites.text: A steep south-facing slope just below Barolo village on the south. Its name means 'rooster's straw' in dialect. Giovanni Canonica, one of the most admired small traditionalists of the 2010s, bottles a celebrated Paiagallo from a hectare of old vines.

sites.name: Coste di Rose
sites.text: A high ridge between Barolo and Monforte with sandy, almost white soils. Coste di Rose wines are pale, perfumed and graceful, a showcase for the sandy end of Barolo's spectrum.

sites.name: Bricco delle Viole
sites.text: The highest point of the Barolo commune, around 450 to 480 m near the chapel of San Pietro delle Viole above the hamlet of Vergne. G.D. Vajra's Bricco delle Viole is the benchmark: ethereal, violet-scented Barolo that has gained in stature as warmer summers favour high sites.

sites.name: Liste
sites.text: A south-facing amphitheatre west of Barolo village below Vergne. Borgogno, the old Barolo house founded in 1761 and revived by the Farinetti family, has made Liste its flagship single vineyard.

sites.name: Fossati
sites.text: Straddling the Barolo and La Morra border north-west of Barolo village, Fossati faces south-east and gives perfumed, mid-weight Barolo. Enzo Boglietti and Dosio bottle it.
sites.class: MGA (Barolo DOCG), Barolo and La Morra

sites.name: Rué
sites.text: A small site between Barolo village and Cannubi, one of the four parcels in Bartolo Mascarello's classic blend. Today Rué is bottled on its own by a few growers.

sites.name: Brunate
sites.text: One of the two or three greatest crus of the western Barolo zone, about 25 ha on a steep south to south-east-facing slope below the little Brunate chapel, straddling the La Morra and Barolo border. Calcareous Sant'Agata marls give wines of depth and structure unusual for La Morra. Giuseppe Rinaldi's Brunate, Roberto Voerzio's and Marcarini's are references; Ceretto and Vietti bottle it too.
sites.class: MGA (Barolo DOCG), La Morra and Barolo

sites.name: Cerequio
sites.text: A natural amphitheatre just west of Brunate, around the restored hamlet of Palais Cerequio. Cerequio's warm, sheltered bowl gives rich, ripe Barolo; Roberto Voerzio's tiny-yield Cerequio was a symbol of the 1990s modernist peak; Michele Chiarlo owns the largest share, and Gaja's Conteisa comes from Cerequio vines bought in 1995.
sites.class: MGA (Barolo DOCG), La Morra and Barolo

sites.name: Rocche dell'Annunziata
sites.text: About 30 ha of steep, crumbling slopes (*rocche*) dropping from the hamlet of Torriglione toward the Annunziata valley. Two sectors, one facing south-east and one south to south-west, on blue marl veined with sand. The wines are the most perfumed and seductive of La Morra, all rose, red cherry and spice. Renato Ratti's Rocche, Paolo Scavino's Rocche dell'Annunziata Riserva and Trediberri are classics.

sites.name: Arborina
sites.text: A gentle, south-east-facing slope north of the Annunziata. Elio Altare's Arborina, from vines near his house, was one of the founding wines of the modernist movement after he cut up his father's old casks with a chainsaw in the early 1980s.

sites.name: Gattera
sites.text: North-east of the Annunziata, where Mauro Veglio and Bovio farm. Gattera wines are generous and early to open.

sites.name: Conca
sites.text: A tiny, south-facing amphitheatre (*conca* means bowl) just below Ratti's Abbazia dell'Annunziata. Renato Ratti's Conca was one of the first single-vineyard Barolos of the 1970s.

sites.name: Serradenari
sites.text: The highest MGA in La Morra, around 500 to 530 m on the ridge south-west of the village. Once thought too cool for Barolo, it now makes taut, fragrant wines prized in hot years.

sites.name: Case Nere
sites.text: On the La Morra side of the Barolo border near Fossati, south-facing. Enzo Boglietti's Case Nere is the best known.

sites.name: Bricco San Biagio
sites.text: A hilltop site east of Santa Maria named after its chapel, giving supple, fragrant wines.

sites.name: Bricco Manzoni
sites.text: Not to be confused with Rocche dei Manzoni in Monforte: a small rise near the hamlet of Manzoni at the eastern edge of La Morra, toward the Castiglione Falletto border.

sites.name: Monprivato
sites.text: About 7 ha on the south-west-facing slope below Castiglione Falletto, almost entirely owned by Giuseppe Mascarello e Figlio. The family bought its first Monprivato vines in 1904 and gradually acquired almost the whole slope; Mauro Mascarello first bottled it alone in 1970. Clay-marl over limestone gives Barolo of exquisite balance and longevity; Ca' d'Morissio, a Riserva from a Michet clone selection, is made only in the greatest years.

sites.name: Villero
sites.text: A large south-west-facing amphitheatre south of Castiglione village with deep marl, considered by many the finest site in the commune. Vietti's Villero Riserva (only in top vintages), Brovia, Giacomo Fenocchio and Boroli bottle it; the wines are powerful yet perfumed, combining the two sides of Barolo's geology.

sites.name: Rocche di Castiglione
sites.text: A narrow escarpment running south from Castiglione Falletto toward Perno, facing south-east above the valley toward Serralunga. The steep, crumbling sandstone and marl give the most elegant, aromatic wines of the commune. Brovia, Vietti, Oddero and Giuseppe Mascarello's former Rocche parcels are famous; Bruno Giacosa's 1978 Rocche is a legend.
sites.class: MGA (Barolo DOCG), Castiglione Falletto and Monforte d'Alba

sites.name: Bricco Boschis
sites.text: The hill north-east of Castiglione Falletto that is essentially the Cavallotto family estate, which they have farmed since 1928 and bottled since 1948. Vigna San Giuseppe, the steep heart, gives their famous Riserva. Cavallotto were early converts to grassed vineyards and natural methods.

sites.name: Fiasco
sites.text: A west-facing slope near Paolo Scavino's winery; Scavino's 'Bric del Fiasc' from here made Enrico Scavino's reputation as a modernist in the 1980s.

sites.name: Mariondino
sites.text: South-west of the village toward Bussia, giving fine, mid-weight wines. Parusso and Armando Parusso farm here.

sites.name: Scarrone
sites.text: Directly below Vietti's cellar in the village, famous for Vietti's old-vine Barbera d'Alba Vigna Scarrone and Vigna Vecchia Scarrone as much as for Nebbiolo.

sites.name: Pira
sites.text: North-west of the village; Roagna's Pira estate, bought in 1989, is a monument of traditional winemaking with very long macerations.

sites.name: Bricco Rocche
sites.text: The top of the Castiglione hill above the Rocche, a Ceretto monopole crowned by their glass tasting cube. Ceretto's Bricco Rocche was one of the first prestige single-vineyard Barolos of the 1980s.

sites.name: Montanello
sites.text: A south-west-facing slope on the road from Castiglione to Monforte, named after the Tenuta Montanello whose 18th-century cellar still stands.

sites.name: Bussia
sites.text: With almost 300 ha, the largest MGA in Barolo and the clearest case of how an MGA is a place name, not a quality rank. It sweeps from the Barolo border through a series of amphitheatres toward Castiglione Falletto. The historic heart, Bussia Soprana with Aldo Conterno's Colonnello, Cicala and Romirasco parcels, faces south-west; outer sectors like Munie are less prized. Prunotto's Bussia (1961) was one of the first single-vineyard Barolos ever labelled.
sites.class: MGA (Barolo DOCG), Monforte d'Alba and Barolo

sites.name: Ginestra
sites.text: A broad, south to south-east-facing amphitheatre east of Monforte village at 300 to 450 m, on compact Serravallian sandstone and marl. Ginestra wines are deep, dark and long-lived. Its sub-sites are famous in their own right: Domenico Clerico's Ciabot Mentin and Pajana, Elio Grasso's Casa Maté, Conterno Fantino's Sorì Ginestra and Vigna del Gris, Paolo Conterno's Ginestra.

sites.name: Mosconi
sites.text: South of Ginestra near Case Mosconi, rising to about 450 m. Long split among small growers, it became sought-after when Pio Cesare and Conterno Fantino bought in, and is known for broad, structured wines.

sites.name: Castelletto
sites.text: Near the hamlet of Castelletto by Perno, facing east to south-east toward Serralunga. Fortemasso and Giuseppe Mascarello hold vines here.

sites.name: Gramolere
sites.text: A west-facing slope around Cascina Gramolere between Bussia and Castelletto; Giovanni Manzone's Gramolere is the benchmark.

sites.name: Perno
sites.text: A large MGA around the hamlet and castle of Perno in Monforte d'Alba, on slopes falling east toward Serralunga and west toward Bussia. Its best-known vineyard is Santo Stefano, which Giuseppe Mascarello e Figlio now labels Barolo Perno Vigna Santo Stefano, a firmer, more austere counterpart to its Monprivato; Rocche dei Manzoni's Vigna Cappella di Santo Stefano comes from the same hillside.

sites.name: Le Coste di Monforte
sites.text: South-east of Monforte village on high, sandy slopes. Often finer and more floral than the rest of Monforte.

sites.name: Bricco San Pietro
sites.text: A large, high MGA west of Monforte by Bussia San Pietro, rising above 500 m. Increasingly valued for freshness in hot vintages.

sites.name: Francia
sites.text: Giacomo Conterno's 14-ha monopole, bought by Giovanni Conterno in 1974 from the estate of Cascina Francia. The source of Monfortino (since the 1978 vintage) and of Barolo Cascina Francia, now labelled simply 'Francia'. West-facing at about 350 to 430 m on poor Serravallian marl, it gives some of the most structured and long-lived Barolo of all.

sites.name: Arione
sites.text: The southernmost great vineyard of Serralunga, next to Francia. Roberto Conterno bought most of it from the Gigi Rosso family in 2015, releasing Barolo Arione from 2015; the purchase was the headline land deal of that decade.

sites.name: Falletto
sites.text: Bruno Giacosa's estate vineyard, bought in 1982, south of Serralunga village. The upper sector gives Le Rocche del Falletto, whose Riserva (red label) is among the most coveted Barolos made. Falletto's calcareous marl gives austere, slow-maturing wines that Giacosa crafted in large oak.

sites.name: Vignarionda
sites.text: About 10 ha of south to south-west-facing amphitheatre at around 330 m south of Serralunga village, on calcareous marl. Long regarded as Serralunga's greatest cru; Massolino's Vigna Rionda Riserva, Oddero, Luigi Pira, Giacomo Anselma and Arnaldo Rivera bottle it. The wines are dense, mineral and very long-lived.

sites.name: Lazzarito
sites.text: An elevated, sheltered site south-east of the village with marked limestone. Its name may come from a lazaretto (plague hospital). Fontanafredda is the main owner (Vigna La Delizia); Vietti, Ettore Germano and Guido Porro (whose lower parcel is Lazzairasco) also bottle it. The wines are perfumed yet firm.

sites.name: Ornato
sites.text: Around the hamlet of Ornato south of the village, south-west facing. Pio Cesare's Ornato, first released in 1985, made it famous.

sites.name: Cerretta
sites.text: A long ridge in the north of Serralunga around the hamlet of Cerretta, at 300 to 400 m. Ettore Germano, Giovanni Rosso and Elio Altare (who bought in 2007) make powerful, tannic Cerretta.

sites.name: Parafada
sites.text: A west-facing slope north of the village around Cascina Parafada, giving rich, ripe Serralunga. Massolino's Parafada is the reference.

sites.name: Badarina
sites.text: A high, south-east-facing site in the south-east of the commune toward Roddino. Bruna Grimaldi's Badarina is the best-known bottling.

sites.name: Briccolina
sites.text: A small, steep slope near Francia in the south of Serralunga, known through Batasiolo's single-vineyard bottling.

sites.name: Gabutti
sites.text: Just east of the village, a site associated with the Cappellano family's Pie Franco and Pie Rupestris bottlings (from ungrafted and grafted vines) and with Gabutti-Boasso.

sites.name: Prapò
sites.text: A steep, south-east-facing amphitheatre in the north-east of Serralunga. Ceretto, Ettore Germano and Schiavenza bottle it.

sites.name: Marenca
sites.text: Just north-west of the village, adjoining Margheria; Luigi Pira's Marenca is the classic.

sites.name: Margheria
sites.text: West-facing, just below Serralunga's castle, sandier and gentler than most of the commune. Massolino and Luigi Pira bottle it.

sites.name: Baudana
sites.text: In the north of Serralunga around the hamlet of Baudana, with mixed exposures. Luigi Baudana's small estate, now owned by G.D. Vajra, made it famous.

sites.name: Boscareto
sites.text: South-east of the village on high ground; Batasiolo and Ferdinando Principiano bottle it.

sites.name: Fontanafredda
sites.text: The MGA surrounding the former royal estate at the northern tip of Serralunga, mostly owned by Fontanafredda itself.

sites.name: Sorano
sites.text: A small MGA by the hamlet of Sorano that crosses into Diano d'Alba, one of the few Barolo crus shared with Diano.
sites.class: MGA (Barolo DOCG), Serralunga d'Alba and Diano d'Alba

sites.name: Monvigliero
sites.text: The grand cru of Verduno: a south-facing slope east of the village, on the Tanaro side of the zone, with sandy Tortonian marl. Its wines are perfumed, spicy and transparent, with famous whole-cluster interpretations by G.B. Burlotto. Paolo Scavino, Castello di Verduno, Bel Colle and Fratelli Alessandria also make it, and its price and prestige have soared since the 2000s.

sites.name: Massara
sites.text: South-west of Verduno toward La Morra; Castello di Verduno's Massara is the main bottling.

sites.name: Breri
sites.text: A slope by the hamlet of Breri east of Verduno, close to Roddi.

sites.name: Ravera
sites.text: A high ridge east of Novello at 380 to 450 m, bordering Barolo's Terlo. Elvio Cogno's estate sits on it, and Vietti's Ravera (first vintage 2008) quickly became one of their top wines. Cool, calcareous and windswept, Ravera gives tense, aromatic Barolo.

sites.name: Panerole
sites.text: Below the hamlet of Panerole east of Novello, a high, fresh site.

sites.name: Castello
sites.text: The vineyard below the castle of Grinzane Cavour, where Cavour managed the family estate and, with the help of Paolo Francesco Staglieno, made some of the first dry, cellar-aged Barolo in the 1830s and 1840s.

sites.name: Garretti
sites.text: On the western edge of Grinzane toward Gallo d'Alba; one of the lower, warmer MGAs of the zone.

sites.name: Bricco Ambrogio
sites.text: The only MGA in Roddi, a south-facing hill above the Tanaro near the castle. Paolo Scavino's Bricco Ambrogio showed what Roddi could do.

sites.name: Mantoetto
sites.text: The only MGA in Cherasco, the westernmost and smallest outpost of Barolo, near the confluence of the Tanaro and Stura.

sites.name: Asili
sites.text: About 14 ha of south-west-facing slope at 200 to 270 m south of Barbaresco village, on silty loam, clay and sand over marl. Asili is the most perfumed of the great Barbaresco crus, all violets and silk. Bruno Giacosa's red-label Asili Riserva, Ceretto's Bricco Asili, Produttori del Barbaresco's Riserva and Ca' del Baio are classics.

sites.name: Rabajà
sites.text: About 20 ha facing south and south-west south of Asili and Martinenga, on limestone with sand and clay. Rabajà gives a fuller, more muscular Barbaresco than Asili, with black cherry and spice. Bruno Rocca's winery sits in it, and Produttori, Giuseppe Cortese, Castello di Verduno and Cascina Luisin bottle it.

sites.name: Martinenga
sites.text: A 12-ha amphitheatre between Asili and Rabajà, a monopole of the Marchesi di Grésy since the 18th century. Its two best parcels, Camp Gros and Gaiun, are bottled as Riservas.

sites.name: Montestefano
sites.text: A steep, south-facing slope east of the village with high calcium content, giving the most structured and tannic wines of Barbaresco. Prunotto released the first labelled Montestefano in 1961; Produttori del Barbaresco and Serafino Rivella are references.

sites.name: Montefico
sites.text: North-east of the village, adjoining Montestefano, on white calcareous marl. Tight and mineral; Roagna's Montefico Vecchie Viti and the Produttori Riserva are benchmarks.

sites.name: Ovello
sites.text: North-west of the village above the Tanaro, cooler and later-ripening. Produttori del Barbaresco and Cantina del Pino make classic Ovello.

sites.name: Pora
sites.text: West of Asili, south-west facing, a lighter, fragrant style. Produttori bottles a Pora Riserva and Ca' del Baio a Pora.

sites.name: Rio Sordo
sites.text: West of Rabajà on the slope down to the 'silent stream' (*rio sordo*) toward Treiso, with sandier soils. Produttori, Cascina Bruciata and Brovia bottle it.

sites.name: Pajè
sites.text: Just south-west of the village. Roagna's Pajè is one of the great old-school Barbarescos, and Produttori makes a Pajè Riserva.

sites.name: Muncagota
sites.text: South of Barbaresco village, between Asili and Rabajà, on steep slopes. Produttori del Barbaresco bottles a Muncagota Riserva in good years, and the Minuto family's Moccagatta estate stands inside the MGA.

sites.name: Secondine
sites.text: Between the village and Asili, the source of Gaja's Sorì San Lorenzo, a south-facing parcel the Gajas bought in 1964 that took its name from the patron saint of Alba's cathedral, which once owned it.

sites.name: Roncaglie
sites.text: West of the village toward the Tanaro, home of Gaja's Sorì Tildin, named after Angelo Gaja's grandmother Clotilde Rey.

sites.name: Faset
sites.text: North of the village, sloping toward the Tanaro; Bottega and Castello di Verduno farm here.

sites.name: Tre Stelle
sites.text: Around the hamlet of Tre Stelle in the south of the commune; Sottimano's and Rizzi's parcels nearby.

sites.name: Gallina
sites.text: A south-facing hill west of Neive village that gives rich, ripe wines; La Spinetta's Gallina, Ugo Lequio and Oddero's Gallina are the best known.

sites.name: Albesani
sites.text: A large MGA north-west of Neive, south-facing. It contains the vineyard of Santo Stefano, made famous by Bruno Giacosa and owned by Castello di Neive, as well as Cantina del Pino and Piero Busso holdings.

sites.name: Starderi
sites.text: North of Neive around the hamlet of Starderi, the source of La Spinetta's Starderi.

sites.name: Serraboella
sites.text: East of Neive near Bricco di Neive; Cigliuti and Paitin (whose Sorì Paitin is here) are the reference estates.

sites.name: Cottà
sites.text: On the Neive side of the border with Barbaresco, near the hamlet of Cottà, south-west facing. Sottimano's Cottà is the classic.

sites.name: Currà
sites.text: A small, steep, south-west-facing site in Neive near the Barbaresco border, next to Gallina, on sandy marl. Sottimano and Bruno Rocca bottle Currà as an intense, spicy single-vineyard Barbaresco.

sites.name: Basarin
sites.text: South of Neive on high ground; Adriano Marco e Vittorio and Moccagatta bottle it.

sites.name: Bricco di Neive
sites.text: The high hill east of Neive at around 400 m, one of the coolest spots in the zone.

sites.name: Pajorè
sites.text: Treiso's most historic cru, on the border with Barbaresco, famed in the 19th century. Sottimano and Rizzi have restored its reputation; Gaja's Sorì Tildin and the Giacosa family once bought grapes here.

sites.name: Marcarini
sites.text: Around the hamlet of Marcarini near Ferrere, home of Ca' del Baio and of Ada Nada's vines.

sites.name: Nervo
sites.text: A high west-facing slope in Treiso toward San Rocco Seno d'Elvio, known for fresh, sinewy wines.

sites.name: Rizzi
sites.text: The MGA around the Dellapiana family's Rizzi estate, a source of lean, perfumed Treiso Barbaresco.

sites.name: Cantina Pertinace
sites.text: The Treiso cooperative founded in 1973 by Mario Barbero and 12 fellow growers, now about 20 members farming some 110 ha. It takes its name from the hamlet of Pertinace, by tradition the birthplace of the Roman emperor Publius Helvius Pertinax (reigned AD 193), and bottles single-MGA Barbaresco from Marcarini, Nervo and Castellizzano.

sites.name: Meruzzano
sites.text: The southernmost part of the Barbaresco zone around the hamlet of Meruzzano, high and cool at up to 450 m.

sites.name: Giacomo Conterno
sites.text: The most revered name in Barolo, based in Monforte d'Alba. Giacomo Conterno started bottling in the 1920s; his son Giovanni bought the Cascina Francia vineyard in Serralunga in 1974, and grandson Roberto (since 2004) added Cerretta (2008), Arione (2015) and Nervi in Gattinara (2018). Monfortino Riserva, aged up to seven years in large casks, is Italy's most sought-after red.

sites.name: Bartolo Mascarello
sites.text: The small cellar on Via Roma in Barolo village where Bartolo Mascarello (1926 to 2005), the 'last of the Mohicans', blended Cannubi, San Lorenzo, Rué and Rocche dell'Annunziata into a single Barolo and drew hand-painted labels reading 'No Barrique, No Berlusconi'. His daughter Maria Teresa keeps the style unchanged.

sites.name: Giuseppe Rinaldi
sites.text: The family cellar at the edge of Barolo village, a citadel of tradition run by Beppe 'Citrico' Rinaldi until his death in 2018 and now by his daughters Marta and Carlotta. Brunate, Tre Tine (Cannubi San Lorenzo, Ravera, Le Coste), Bussia and Rocche dell'Annunziata are fermented in old wooden vats and aged in large casks.

sites.name: Giuseppe Mascarello e Figlio
sites.text: Based in Monchiero, just outside the Barolo zone, with cellars dating to the 18th century, once used to store ice. Mauro Mascarello and his son Giuseppe make Monprivato, Ca' d'Morissio, Villero and Perno Vigna Santo Stefano in large casks; among the purest expressions of Castiglione Falletto.

sites.name: Bruno Giacosa
sites.text: The Neive cellar of Bruno Giacosa (1929 to 2018), who made legendary Barbaresco and Barolo first from bought grapes (Santo Stefano, Asili, Rabajà, Rocche di Castiglione) and later from his own Falletto and Asili. His red labels (Riservas) are among the greatest Nebbiolos of the 20th century. His daughter Bruna runs it today.

sites.name: Vietti
sites.text: Founded in Castiglione Falletto in the 19th century; Alfredo Currado (1932 to 2010) married into the family and made it famous, bottling single-vineyard Barolos from the 1960s and rescuing Arneis. Since 2016 it has been owned by the Krause family of Iowa; Luca Currado left in 2023. The cellar burrows under the village.

sites.name: Cavallotto (Tenuta Bricco Boschis)
sites.text: The Cavallotto family's estate on Bricco Boschis in Castiglione Falletto, farmed since 1928 and bottled since 1948. Classic, long-macerated Barolo from Bricco Boschis Vigna San Giuseppe and Vignolo, and a pioneering green-cover, low-chemical approach from the 1970s.

sites.name: G.B. Burlotto
sites.text: Verduno's historic house, founded by Giovan Battista Burlotto, who supplied the House of Savoy and won medals in the 1880s. Fabio Alessandria's whole-cluster, foot-trodden Monvigliero turned it into one of the most sought-after Barolos of the 2010s; it also makes the benchmark Verduno Pelaverga.

sites.name: Roberto Voerzio
sites.text: La Morra estate founded in 1986 by Roberto Voerzio, known for extreme green-harvesting (sometimes under 500 grams of grapes per vine) and modern but site-driven wines from Brunate, Cerequio, Rocche dell'Annunziata-Torriglione and Sarmassa.

sites.name: Elio Altare
sites.text: The Annunziata estate where Elio Altare, after visiting Burgundy in the 1970s, took a chainsaw to his father's old casks and launched Barolo's modernist movement. His daughter Silvia now runs it; Arborina and Cerretta are the crus.

sites.name: Renato Ratti (Abbazia dell'Annunziata)
sites.text: Renato Ratti (1934 to 1988) drew the first map of Barolo's historic crus in the 1970s, launched Rocche and Conca single-vineyard wines and founded the wine museum in the former Benedictine Abbey of the Annunziata. The family's modern cellar is nearby.

sites.name: Gaja
sites.text: The Barbaresco house founded in 1859 and transformed by Angelo Gaja from the 1960s with single-vineyard Barbaresco (Sorì San Lorenzo 1967, Sorì Tildin 1970, Costa Russi 1978), barriques, Chardonnay and Cabernet in the Langhe, and global marketing. The family later bought Barolo vineyards (Sperss in Serralunga, Conteisa in La Morra), plus estates in Tuscany and on Etna.

sites.name: Produttori del Barbaresco
sites.text: The cooperative founded in 1958 by Don Fiorino Marengo, heir to Domizio Cavazza's 1894 Cantina Sociale. Its members farm roughly 100 ha; in great years it bottles nine single-MGA Riservas (Asili, Montefico, Montestefano, Muncagota, Ovello, Pajè, Pora, Rabajà, Rio Sordo), one of the best-value collections of great Nebbiolo anywhere.

sites.name: Castello Falletti and WiMu wine museum
sites.text: The castle of the Falletti marquises in Barolo village, where Juliette Colbert, Marchesa di Barolo, presided over the estate in the 19th century. Today it houses the WiMu wine museum and the Enoteca Regionale del Barolo in its cellars.

sites.name: Marchesi di Barolo
sites.text: The historic cellars across from the Falletti castle that trace their lineage to Juliette Colbert's estate. After her death in 1864 the Opera Pia Barolo charity inherited it; in 1929 the Abbona family bought the cellars and continue to make Cannubi and Sarmassa.

sites.name: Fontanafredda
sites.text: The royal hunting estate given by King Vittorio Emanuele II to his mistress Rosa Vercellana, 'la Bela Rosin', in 1858; their son Emanuele Alberto began making wine here in 1878. Its striped villa and village of cellars now belong to Oscar Farinetti (of Eataly), who also revived Borgogno and Mirafiore.

sites.name: Castello di Grinzane Cavour
sites.text: The castle where the young Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, future architect of Italian unification, was mayor from 1832 and ran the family estate, hiring Paolo Francesco Staglieno to make dry Barolo. Now home to the Enoteca Regionale Piemontese Cavour and the annual white truffle auction. Part of the UNESCO site.

sites.name: Castello di Verduno
sites.text: Savoy castle bought by King Carlo Alberto in 1838, where royal winemakers worked with Nebbiolo; today a hotel and winery run by the Burlotto-Bianco family, making Monvigliero, Massara and Barbaresco Rabajà.

sites.name: Massolino
sites.text: Family estate in the centre of Serralunga, founded 1896; makers of Vigna Rionda Riserva, Parafada, Margheria and Parussi.

sites.name: Pio Cesare
sites.text: Founded in 1881 inside Alba's old town, with cellars built on Roman walls. One of the few houses that still blend Barolo from several communes, alongside single-vineyard Ornato and Barbaresco Il Bricco.

sites.name: Ceretto
sites.text: Bruno and Marcello Ceretto turned their father's merchant house into a pioneer of single-vineyard Barolo and Barbaresco (Bricco Rocche, Brunate, Prapò, Bricco Asili) from the 1970s. Their hilltop headquarters at Monsordo Bernardina outside Alba features the 'Acino' glass bubble.

sites.name: Elvio Cogno
sites.text: The Novello estate on the Ravera hill founded by Elvio Cogno, former winemaker at Marcarini. Now run by Nadia Cogno and Valter Fissore, it revived the Nascetta grape and makes the Ravera Riserva Vigna Elena from the Rosé clone of Nebbiolo.

sites.name: Conterno Fantino
sites.text: Monforte estate (1982) on the Ginestra hill, known for Sorì Ginestra and Vigna del Gris.

sites.name: Elio Grasso
sites.text: Family estate in the Ginestra amphitheatre, makers of Ginestra Casa Maté and Gavarini Chiniera, and Runcot Riserva.

sites.name: Paolo Scavino
sites.text: Castiglione Falletto house (1921) that Enrico Scavino turned into a modernist star in the 1980s; now run by his daughters with holdings in 20 MGAs including Bric del Fiasc, Rocche dell'Annunziata, Monvigliero and Cannubi.

sites.name: Luciano Sandrone
sites.text: Luciano Sandrone's 1978 debut made in a garage while he was cellar master at Marchesi di Barolo. Famous for Aleste (Cannubi Boschis) and Le Vigne, a blend of four communes.

sites.name: Borgogno
sites.text: Founded 1761 in Barolo village and famous for its huge library of old vintages; bought by Oscar Farinetti in 2008 and returned to concrete and large-cask tradition, with Cannubi and Liste at the top.

sites.name: Produttori di Terre del Barolo
sites.text: The Barolo zone's big cooperative, founded in 1958 by Arnaldo Rivera, mayor of Castiglione Falletto; its premium line carries his name.

sites.name: Abbazia dell'Annunziata (Ratti wine museum)
sites.text: The 15th-century Benedictine abbey at the Annunziata where Renato Ratti opened the Museo Ratti dei Vini d'Alba in the 1970s, telling the story of Barolo's winemaking.

sites.name: Belvedere di La Morra
sites.text: The terrace at the top of La Morra, at about 513 m, with the most famous panorama of the Barolo hills, the Alps beyond and, on clear days, Monviso.

sites.name: Castello di Serralunga d'Alba
sites.text: A 14th-century donjon castle of the Falletti family that dominates the village and gives Serralunga its silhouette.

sites.name: Aldo Conterno
sites.text: Founded in 1969 when Aldo Conterno split from his brother Giovanni of Giacomo Conterno. The Bussia Soprana estate makes Colonnello, Cicala, Romirasco and the Granbussia Riserva blend.

sites.name: G.D. Vajra
sites.text: Aldo Vaira's estate at Vergne, high on the Barolo commune, makers of Bricco delle Viole and Ravera Barolos and revivers of Freisa and Riesling in the Langhe.

sites.name: Oddero
sites.text: Santa Maria di La Morra estate whose family has farmed since the 18th century; one of the first to bottle Barolo (1878). Holdings in Vignarionda, Villero, Rocche di Castiglione, Brunate and Bussia.

sites.name: Roagna
sites.text: Barbaresco house run by Luca Roagna, champion of ultra-long macerations and old-vine selections (Pajè, Montefico, Asili, Faset) plus the Pira estate in Castiglione Falletto.

sites.name: Marchesi di Grésy (Martinenga)
sites.text: The Cisa Asinari family estate, owners of the Martinenga monopole since the 18th century; bottling since 1973.

sites.name: Castello di Neive
sites.text: The 18th-century castle of Neive, whose cellars hold Santo Stefano Barbaresco from the Albesani MGA, the vineyard Bruno Giacosa made famous from bought grapes in the 1960s and 1970s. Count Guido Stupino also revived Arneis plantings here in the 1960s.

sites.name: Torre di Barbaresco
sites.text: The 11th-century watchtower above the Tanaro, 36 metres tall, symbol of Barbaresco village and its viewing platform over the vineyards.

sites.name: Enoteca Regionale del Barbaresco
sites.text: Barbaresco's regional wine shop and tasting room inside the deconsecrated church of San Donato in the village.

sites.name: Scuola Enologica di Alba (Istituto Umberto I)
sites.text: The Royal Oenological School founded in Alba in 1881 with Domizio Cavazza as director; it trained generations of Piedmontese winemakers, including many of today's Barolo producers.
producers: Scuola Enologica di Alba (Istituto Umberto I)

sites.name: Agenzia di Pollenzo (University of Gastronomic Sciences)
sites.text: The neo-Gothic Savoy royal estate at Pollenzo, restored by Slow Food founder Carlo Petrini's movement; home since 2004 of the University of Gastronomic Sciences and the Banca del Vino, a wine library of Italian bottles.
producers: Agenzia di Pollenzo (University of Gastronomic Sciences)

sites.name: Ca' del Baio
sites.text: Treiso family estate of the Grasso family, makers of Asili, Pora and Vallegrande Barbaresco.

sites.name: Fratelli Cigliuti
sites.text: Small family estate on the Serraboella hill in Neive, bottling its own Barbaresco since 1964; Renato Cigliuti's daughters now make classic Serraboella and Vie Erte from the family's south-facing slopes.

sites.name: Albino Rocca
sites.text: Barbaresco family estate founded by Albino Rocca and now run by his granddaughters, with Ovello Vigna Loreto, Ronchi and Cottà among its single-MGA Barbarescos, made in large casks in a fresh, fine-boned style.

sites.name: Moccagatta
sites.text: The Minuto family's estate in the Muncagota MGA south of Barbaresco village, making Bric Balin and Basarin.

sites.name: Underground cathedrals of Canelli
sites.text: Kilometres of brick-vaulted tunnels dug into the Canelli hill by Gancia, Bosca, Contratto and Coppo in the 19th century to age sparkling wine. Carlo Gancia made Italy's first metodo classico here in 1865. A core zone of the UNESCO site since 2014.

sites.name: Contratto
sites.text: Founded in 1867, one of the oldest sparkling-wine houses in Italy; its cellars are part of the Canelli 'cathedrals'.

sites.name: Gancia
sites.text: Founded by Carlo Gancia, who learned the Champagne method in Reims and made Italy's first sparkling wine in Canelli in 1865, later inventing the sweet Moscato spumante that became Asti.

sites.name: Bosca
sites.text: Canelli sparkling-wine house founded in 1831 whose cellars are part of the UNESCO 'underground cathedrals'.

sites.name: Braida
sites.text: The Rocchetta Tanaro estate where Giacomo Bologna released Bricco dell'Uccellone in 1982, the barrique-aged Barbera that changed the grape's fortunes. His children Raffaella and Giuseppe run it.

sites.name: Vigneti Massa
sites.text: Walter Massa's estate in Monleale, where from 1987 he saved Timorasso from extinction and released the first modern varietal Timorasso. His Costa del Vento and Sterpi crus are benchmarks.

sites.name: La Scolca
sites.text: Gavi estate whose Gavi dei Gavi (black label, first made in the 1960s) created the market for prestige Gavi; owned by the Soldati family since 1919.

sites.name: Carema terraces and pilun
sites.text: The terraced vineyards of Carema with their stone-and-lime pillars (*pilun*) holding wooden pergolas, between the village and the Dora Baltea. The Cantina dei Produttori Nebbiolo di Carema, founded in 1960, is at the foot.

sites.name: Travaglini
sites.text: Gattinara's largest estate, founded in 1920 by Clemente Travaglini; its distinctive curved bottle, designed in 1958 to catch sediment, is an icon of Alto Piemonte.

sites.name: Antoniolo
sites.text: Founded 1948; Rosanna Antoniolo and her children make the reference single-vineyard Gattinaras San Francesco, Osso San Grato and Castelle.

sites.name: Le Piane
sites.text: Christoph Künzli's estate, which from 1998 rescued Boca with the help of the veteran grower Antonio Cerri, whose old maggiorina-trained vines it took over.

sites.name: Proprietà Sperino
sites.text: Paolo De Marchi (Isole e Olena) and his son Luca revived the family's Lessona estate from 1999, restoring a 16th-century cellar.

sites.name: Poderi Luigi Einaudi
sites.text: Founded in 1897 by Luigi Einaudi, economist and later President of Italy, who bought the San Giacomo farm in Dogliani; benchmark Dogliani and Barolo from Cannubi, Terlo and Bussia.

sites.name: Montalbera
sites.text: The largest producer of Ruchè, based at the Cascina Montalbera outside Castagnole Monferrato, with Grignolino and Barbera alongside.

sites.name: Orsolani
sites.text: San Giorgio Canavese estate founded in 1894, the reference for Erbaluce di Caluso and Caluso Passito Sulé.

sites.name: Ecomuseo della Pietra da Cantoni, Cella Monte
sites.text: Cella Monte's eco-museum explains the *infernot*, small cellars carved by hand into the soft Pietra da Cantoni sandstone beneath Monferrato houses to store wine; a core zone of the UNESCO site.
producers: Ecomuseo della Pietra da Cantoni, Cella Monte

sites.name: Morgex and La Salle vineyards
sites.appellation: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle
sites.text: The Prié Blanc vineyards between Morgex and La Salle, at up to about 1,200 m below Mont Blanc's south face. Low pergolas on stone pillars, ungrafted vines and the Cave Mont Blanc cooperative's winery (founded 1983) make this one of Europe's most extreme vineyard landscapes.
producers: Cave Mont Blanc de Morgex et La Salle

sites.name: Enfer d'Arvier
sites.text: The 'hell' of Arvier: a rocky south-facing amphitheatre just above the village where heat reflects off the cliffs, making Petit Rouge ripen far above its usual altitude.

sites.name: Donnas terraces and Roman road
sites.text: The Costa dei vigneti of Donnas: granite terraces of Picotendro (Nebbiolo) on stone-pillared pergolas lining the Roman Via delle Gallie, cut through the rock with a carved milestone arch. The Caves Coopératives de Donnas (1971) vinifies the growers' grapes.

sites.name: Les Crêtes
sites.text: Costantino Charrère's estate at Aymavilles, the valley's most famous private winery. Its barrel-fermented Chardonnay Cuvée Bois and Petite Arvine set the standard; Charrère also rescued Fumin and Prëmetta.

sites.name: Institut Agricole Régional
sites.text: The agricultural institute in Aosta, run for decades by the Canons of the Great St Bernard, whose experimental cellar since 1982 has preserved native grapes like Mayolet, Vuillermin and Cornalin and trained the valley's winemakers.

sites.name: Grosjean
sites.text: Family estate at Ollignan in Quart, one of the first organic producers in the valley, known for Fumin, Cornalin and Petite Arvine.

sites.name: Cinque Terre terraces (Manarola to Corniglia)
sites.text: The terraced slopes between Manarola and Corniglia, the heart of the Cinque Terre wine landscape: dry-stone *fasce* climbing from the sea to about 400 m, with monorails for the harvest. Part of the UNESCO site of Portovenere, Cinque Terre and the islands.

sites.name: Cantina Cinque Terre
sites.text: The growers' cooperative at Groppo above Manarola, founded in 1982 to save the terraces; it makes a large share of the DOC's white and Sciacchetrà.

sites.name: Castello dei Doria, Dolceacqua
sites.text: The ruined castle of the Doria family above Dolceacqua and its humpbacked medieval bridge, painted by Monet in 1884. The town is the heart of Rossese country.

sites.name: Terre Bianche
sites.text: Hilltop estate at Arcagna above Dolceacqua, named for its white marly soils, making benchmark Rossese and Pigato.

sites.name: Luni (Roman Luna)
sites.text: The ruins of Luna, a Roman colony founded in 177 BC that exported Carrara marble and wine; Pliny praised the wine of Luna. Its name lives on in the Colli di Luni DOC and the Lunigiana.

sites.name: Lunae Bosoni
sites.text: The Bosoni family's estate at Castelnuovo Magra, the largest and most influential in Colli di Luni, with Vermentino Etichetta Nera as its flagship.

sites.name: Albenga valleys (Ortovero, Ranzo)
sites.text: The Arroscia and Lerrone valleys inland from Albenga, around Ortovero and Ranzo, the historic home of Pigato.

sites.name: Guido Berlucchi (Palazzo Lana)
sites.text: The historic Palazzo Lana in Borgonato, where in 1961 Franco Ziliani made the first 3,000 bottles of Pinot di Franciacorta by the traditional method for Guido Berlucchi. Still the zone's largest producer.

sites.name: Ca' del Bosco
sites.text: Maurizio Zanella's estate in Erbusco, founded in the 1960s by his mother Annamaria Clementi; its Cuvée Annamaria Clementi Riserva is one of Italy's greatest sparkling wines, and its gate is a giant bronze sun by Arnaldo Pomodoro.

sites.name: Bellavista
sites.text: Founded by Vittorio Moretti in 1977 on the Bellavista hill at Erbusco; with Ca' del Bosco it built Franciacorta's reputation, and its Vittorio Moretti Riserva is a benchmark.

sites.name: Monte Rossa
sites.text: Cazzago San Martino estate founded by Paolo Rabotti and Paola Rovetta in 1972, early champions of Franciacorta's quality rules.

sites.name: Sassella (Santuario della Madonna della Sassella)
sites.text: The 15th-century sanctuary perched on a rock spur among the Sassella terraces west of Sondrio, the emblem of Valtellina's most famous subzone, warm and rocky, giving the most complete wines.

sites.name: Grumello (Castel Grumello)
sites.text: The ruined 13th-century twin castle above Montagna in Valtellina that gives the Grumello subzone its name; the terraces below give fragrant, mid-weight Nebbiolo.

sites.name: Inferno
sites.text: The smallest of the main subzones, a stack of terraces on bare rock east of Sondrio around Poggiridenti and Tresivio, so steep and hot it was named 'hell'. Its wines are dense, mineral and long-lived.

sites.name: Valgella
sites.text: The largest subzone, centred on Teglio and Chiuro in the eastern valley, at higher altitudes, giving lighter, perfumed Nebbiolo.

sites.name: Maroggia
sites.text: The smallest subzone, near Berbenno at the western end of the Valtellina Superiore zone and the most recent of the five to be named on labels.

sites.name: Nino Negri (Castello Quadrio)
sites.text: Valtellina's best-known house, founded in 1897 and based in the 15th-century Castello Quadrio at Chiuro; its 5 Stelle Sfursat, created by Casimiro Maule, defined Sforzato.

sites.name: Arpepe
sites.text: The Pelizzatti Perego family's estate at the foot of the Sassella, with a cellar dug into the rock; its long-aged Sassella, Grumello and Inferno Riservas are reference wines for traditional Valtellina.

sites.name: Ca' dei Frati
sites.text: The Dal Cero family's estate at Lugana di Sirmione, which did more than anyone to make Lugana a serious, age-worthy white.

sites.name: Conte Vistarino
sites.text: The Giorgi di Vistarino family estate at Rocca de' Giorgi, where the counts planted Pinot Noir from France in the 1850s; today it makes single-vineyard Pinot Nero (Pernice, Bertone, Tavernetto) and metodo classico.

sites.name: Frecciarossa
sites.text: Casteggio estate whose Giorgio Odero exported bottled Oltrepò wine to the US in the 1930s, a pioneer of estate bottling in the region.

sites.name: Moscato di Scanzo vineyards
sites.text: The terraced hills of Scanzorosciate above Bergamo, the entire 31-hectare world of Moscato di Scanzo.

sites.name: Gries
sites.text: The historic Lagrein heartland on the alluvial gravels of the Talfer fan in western Bolzano, around the Benedictine Muri-Gries abbey. Hot, sandy and stony, it gives the deepest Lagrein in Alto Adige.

sites.name: Mazon
sites.text: A gently sloping plateau above Egna/Neumarkt at 300 to 450 m, Alto Adige's most famous site for Pinot Noir, with Hofstätter's Barthenau Vigna Sant'Urbano as the benchmark.

sites.name: Eppan Berg
sites.text: The upper slopes of Appiano (Eppan) at 450 to 600 m in the Oltradige, a cool, calcareous-moraine site famous for Pinot Bianco, Sauvignon and Pinot Noir, the backyard of San Michele Appiano and Girlan.

sites.name: Brenntal
sites.text: A 'burnt valley' amphitheatre near Cortaccia (Kurtatsch) famous for warm, ripe Cabernet and Merlot and Cantina Kurtatsch's Brenntal Merlot Riserva.

sites.name: Tramin-Söll
sites.text: The terraced slopes above Termeno (Tramin) around the hamlet of Söll, Gewürztraminer's spiritual home: the variety takes its name from this village, and Cantina Tramin's Nussbaumer comes from these parts.

sites.name: Tramin-Rungg
sites.text: Ronchi, the hillside hamlet south of Termeno, home of Elena Walch and of old Gewürztraminer pergolas.

sites.name: St. Justina
sites.text: The steep hamlet of Santa Giustina on Bolzano's eastern slopes, a classic core site of St. Magdalener Schiava.

sites.name: Leitach
sites.text: Leitach on the hillside above Bolzano's Rencio district, part of the St. Magdalener classico area, known for Schiava and Lagrein on porphyry and moraine.

sites.name: Prazöll
sites.text: A St. Magdalener classico hamlet on the slopes above Bolzano, among the steepest of the subzone, with old pergola-trained Schiava and a little Lagrein giving fragrant, almond-scented reds.

sites.name: Rentsch
sites.text: Rencio, on Bolzano's eastern edge, a historic Lagrein and Schiava hamlet at the foot of St. Magdalena.

sites.name: Gries-Moritzing
sites.text: San Maurizio on the western edge of Bolzano, where Cantina Bolzano built its new winery in 2018 into the hillside.

sites.name: Girlan
sites.text: Cornaiano in the Oltradige, the Schiava and Pinot Noir village of the Girlan cooperative, on moraine slopes at about 400 to 500 m.

sites.name: Montiggl
sites.text: Monticolo between the two Monticolo lakes above Appiano, on porphyry and moraine, a cool white-wine site.

sites.name: St. Josef
sites.text: San Giuseppe al Lago on the shore of Lake Caldaro, warm and sheltered, the core of Kalterersee Classico; Manincor's estate lies here.

sites.name: Siebeneich
sites.text: Settequerce between Bolzano and Terlano on the floor of the Adige valley, hot alluvium suited to Lagrein and red Bordeaux varieties.

sites.name: Sirmian
sites.text: Sirmiano above Nalles on the west side of the valley, cool porphyry slopes for whites.

sites.name: Vorberg
sites.text: The porphyry hillside above Terlano that gives the Cantina Terlano's famous Pinot Bianco Riserva Vorberg.

sites.name: Kreuth
sites.text: A Terlano hillside site whose name appears on Cantina Terlano's Chardonnay Kreuth.

sites.name: Nafen
sites.text: A steep, high site near Bressanone in the Valle Isarco, on schist and moraine, giving taut, aromatic whites such as Kerner, Sylvaner and Grüner Veltliner.

sites.name: Brixner
sites.text: The vineyards around Bressanone (Brixen), including those of the Abbazia di Novacella, the northernmost UGA cluster in Italy.

sites.name: Tirol
sites.text: The hillside of Tirolo above Merano, beneath Castel Tirolo, the castle that gave its name to the whole Tyrol.

sites.name: Naturnser
sites.text: The south-facing slopes of Naturno at the mouth of Val Venosta, a dry rain-shadow valley where Pinot Noir and Riesling ripen slowly on gneiss and schist.

sites.name: Kastelbeller
sites.text: Castelbello in Val Venosta, home of Falkenstein's taut Riesling and Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Cantina Terlano
sites.text: Founded in 1893, one of the great white-wine producers of Europe. Its legendary Pinot Bianco and Sauvignon from porphyry soils age for decades, and the 'Rarity' releases have spent ten or more years on the lees.

sites.name: Cantina Tramin
sites.text: Termeno's cooperative, housed since 2010 in a striking green-steel building by Werner Tscholl; its Nussbaumer and Epokale Gewürztraminers are reference wines for the grape in its namesake village.

sites.name: Termeno / Tramin
sites.text: The village that gave its name to the Traminer family of grapes, including Gewürztraminer; documents from the 13th century mention Traminer wine.

sites.name: Abbazia di Novacella (Kloster Neustift)
sites.text: Augustinian canons' abbey founded in 1142 near Bressanone, with vineyards and a winery that is the reference for Valle Isarco Sylvaner, Kerner and Grüner Veltliner.

sites.name: Abbazia Muri-Gries
sites.text: Benedictine monastery in Bolzano's Gries district since 1845, whose monks make some of the finest Lagrein from the surrounding gravels.

sites.name: Cantina San Michele Appiano
sites.text: Founded in 1907, made famous by winemaker Hans Terzer from 1977 with the Sanct Valentin line, especially Sauvignon.

sites.name: Kellerei Kaltern
sites.text: Caldaro's merged cooperative, formed from the village's historic co-ops, which leads the quality revival of Kalterersee Schiava and also makes the Quintessenz range of sweet and still wines.

sites.name: Lake Caldaro (Kalterer See)
sites.text: The warmest bathing lake in the Alps, ringed by Schiava vineyards that give the Kalterersee Classico.
sites.class: Classico zone of Lago di Caldaro DOC

sites.name: St. Magdalena church, Bolzano
sites.text: The little Gothic church on the hill above Bolzano surrounded by Schiava pergolas, symbol of the Santa Maddalena subzone.
sites.class: Heart of the Santa Maddalena Classico zone

sites.name: Castel Juval
sites.text: Reinhold Messner's castle at the mouth of the Val Senales, with terraced vineyards farmed by the Aurich family under the Unterortl label.

sites.name: J. Hofstätter
sites.text: Termeno estate founded in 1907, owner of the Barthenau estate in Mazon (Pinot Noir Vigna Sant'Urbano) and the Kolbenhof Gewürztraminer.

sites.name: Ferrari (Cantine Ferrari)
sites.text: Founded by Giulio Ferrari in 1902 and owned by the Lunelli family since 1952; Italy's best-known metodo classico house, with cellars at Ravina south of Trento.

sites.name: Villa Margon (Ferrari)
sites.text: Lunelli family's 16th-century villa above Ravina with frescoes of Charles V, now Ferrari's hospitality house among its vineyards.

sites.name: Foradori
sites.text: Elisabetta Foradori's biodynamic estate in Mezzolombardo, where she restored Teroldego's clonal diversity and makes amphora-fermented Teroldego and Nosiola.

sites.name: Campo Rotaliano
sites.text: The flat gravel triangle between Mezzolombardo, Mezzocorona and San Michele, where the Noce meets the Adige; Teroldego's only true home, walled by cliffs on three sides.

sites.name: Fondazione Edmund Mach (Istituto Agrario San Michele all'Adige)
sites.text: Founded in 1874 in an Augustinian monastery by the Tyrolean Diet, with Edmund Mach as first director; one of Europe's leading vine-research centres, whose researchers published one of the first draft sequences of the grapevine (Pinot Noir) genome in 2007.

sites.name: Tenuta San Leonardo
sites.text: The Guerrieri Gonzaga family's estate near Avio in the Vallagarina, whose Bordeaux-blend San Leonardo is one of Italy's classic reds.

sites.name: Pojer e Sandri
sites.text: Faedo estate founded in 1975 by Mario Pojer and Fiorentino Sandri, pioneers of mountain Müller-Thurgau and sparkling wine.

sites.name: Foscarino
sites.text: The volcanic hill north of Monteforte d'Alpone, crowned by the Monte Foscarino, the most famous name in Soave: black basalt soils give smoky, saline, structured Garganega. Anselmi's Capitel Foscarino, Inama's Vigneti di Foscarino and Gini's Contrada Salvarenza come from here.

sites.name: Froscà
sites.text: Volcanic slopes between Soave and Monteforte, where Gini's 1900s-planted vines give one of the zone's deepest wines.

sites.name: Castelcerino
sites.text: The highest village of the Soave Classico zone at about 400 m, cooler and windswept, on mixed volcanic and limestone soils.

sites.name: Fittà
sites.text: A hamlet high in the Classico zone north of Soave, on volcanic soils, where Suavia and Filippi have vineyards.

sites.name: Monte Grande
sites.text: A volcanic hill east of Soave, the source of Graziano Prà's acclaimed Monte Grande Soave, partly made with dried grapes.

sites.name: Pressoni
sites.text: Steep slopes north of Soave on volcanic and limestone soils; Cantina di Soave's Rocca Sveva line and several growers bottle it.

sites.name: Carbonare
sites.text: A high volcanic site in the Classico zone known through Suavia's Monte Carbonare, a benchmark of saline, long-lived Garganega.

sites.name: Volpare
sites.text: Hillside slopes near Castelcerino in the north of the Classico zone, cooler and higher than the valley floor, giving fine, fragrant Garganega.

sites.name: Costalunga
sites.text: Volcanic hills around the hamlets of Brognoligo and Costalunga east of Monteforte d'Alpone, with dark basalt soils that give smoky, saline Soave.

sites.name: Brognoligo
sites.text: A hamlet in the Alpone valley north-east of Monteforte, on dark volcanic soils.

sites.name: Duello
sites.text: One of the two eastern UGAs near Roncà, on volcanic basalt outside the Classico zone.

sites.name: Roncà - Monte Calvarina
sites.text: The eastern volcanic UGA rising to the Monte Calvarina, an Eocene volcanic peak north of Roncà; cool and high.

sites.name: Monte di Colognola
sites.text: One of the three western UGAs on limestone above Colognola ai Colli, outside the Classico zone.

sites.name: Calvarino (Pieropan)
sites.text: Not an official UGA name but the most famous single vineyard of Soave: Pieropan's Calvarino ('little Calvary', for how hard it is to work), first bottled separately in 1971 and one of Italy's great white wines, on basalt and tuff north of Soave.

sites.name: Castello di Soave
sites.text: The Scaliger castle of the 10th to 14th centuries and the walls enclosing the town of Soave, overlooking the Classico vineyards.

sites.name: Pieropan
sites.text: Founded in 1880 in the centre of Soave; Leonildo Pieropan made the first single-vineyard Soave (Calvarino 1971, La Rocca 1978) and helped restore Soave's reputation.

sites.name: Giuseppe Quintarelli
sites.text: The Cerè estate above Negrar where Giuseppe 'Bepi' Quintarelli (1927 to 2012) made the most revered Amarone and Recioto, dried on racks in the attic and aged up to eight years in old casks. His handwritten labels are icons. The family continues his work.

sites.name: Romano Dal Forno
sites.text: Romano Dal Forno's estate at Lodoletta in the Val d'Illasi, outside the Classico zone. After apprenticing with Quintarelli he created a monumental, ultra-concentrated Amarone, dried in a ventilated fruttaio and aged in new barriques.

sites.name: Bertani (Villa Mosconi Bertani)
sites.text: Founded in 1857 by the Bertani brothers; its Amarone Classico, aged six years or more in large casks, is the benchmark of the traditional style. The company's Grezzana site and the 18th-century Villa Mosconi Bertani at Arbizzano anchor its history.

sites.name: Serego Alighieri and Masi (Gargagnago)
sites.text: The estate at Gargagnago bought in 1353 by Pietro, son of Dante Alighieri, still owned by his descendants the Counts Serego Alighieri and made in partnership with Masi, whose headquarters are in the same village. Masi revived Ripasso with Campofiorin in 1964.

sites.name: Allegrini
sites.text: Fumane family estate whose La Poja (1983, pure Corvina from a hilltop vineyard) and Amarone helped modernise Valpolicella; the family also restored the Renaissance Villa della Torre.

sites.name: Villa della Torre
sites.text: A 16th-century Mannerist villa at Fumane with grotesque fireplaces attributed to Giulio Romano's circle, now owned by the Allegrini family.

sites.name: Pieve di San Giorgio di Valpolicella
sites.text: The Romanesque parish church at San Giorgio di Valpolicella, built on early-medieval foundations and containing a Lombard-era ciborium inscription from the 8th century, a reminder of how old the valley's Christian and winemaking communities are.

sites.name: Tommaso Bussola
sites.text: Self-taught grower in San Peretto di Negrar, famous for opulent Recioto and Amarone TB.

sites.name: Cartizze
sites.text: 107 hectares of very steep slopes between San Pietro di Barbozza, Santo Stefano and Saccol in Valdobbiadene: the grand cru of Prosecco, traditionally made Dry, with ripe pear and floral richness.

sites.name: Le Colline del Prosecco di Conegliano e Valdobbiadene
sites.text: The hogback hills between Valdobbiadene and Vittorio Veneto, with grassy *ciglioni* terraces and a patchwork of woods and vines, inscribed as a cultural landscape in 2019.

sites.name: Scuola Enologica G.B. Cerletti, Conegliano
sites.text: Founded in 1876, Italy's first school of viticulture and oenology; its teachers shaped modern Prosecco technique, and its headmaster Luigi Manzoni bred the Manzoni crossings, including Incrocio Manzoni 6.0.13, in the 1920s and 1930s.

sites.name: Nino Franco
sites.text: Founded in Valdobbiadene in 1919; Primo Franco's Rustico and Grave di Stecca made it one of the first Prosecco houses with an international reputation for quality.

sites.name: Bisol
sites.text: A family growing grapes in Valdobbiadene since 1542, with the largest share of Cartizze; with a majority stake owned since 2014 by the Lunelli family of Ferrari.

sites.name: Villa Sandi
sites.text: A 17th-century villa in Palladian style at Crocetta del Montello with kilometres of underground tunnels from the First World War, now the Moretti Polegato family's Prosecco house.

sites.name: Prosecco (Trieste)
sites.text: The Karst village above Trieste, in Friuli Venezia Giulia, that gave its name to Prosecco; its inclusion in the 2009 DOC is what allowed Italy to protect the name as a geographical indication.
sites.class: Village that gave its name to the wine

sites.name: Maculan
sites.text: Fausto Maculan's Breganze estate, maker of Torcolato and the botrytised Acininobili from Vespaiola.

sites.name: Vignalta
sites.text: Arquà Petrarca estate whose Gemola Merlot-Cabernet showed the volcanic Euganean Hills' potential.

sites.name: Arquà Petrarca
sites.text: The hill village where the poet Petrarch spent his last years and died in 1374; he kept a vineyard and praised the Euganean wines.

sites.name: Gravner
sites.text: Josko Gravner's estate at Lenzuolo Bianco, Oslavia, on the Slovenian border. After fame for modern barrel-fermented whites, he turned in 1997 to long skin maceration and, from 2001, to Georgian clay *qvevri* buried in his cellar, making amber Ribolla Gialla that ages seven years before release. He is the godfather of modern orange wine.

sites.name: Radikon
sites.text: Stanko Radikon (1953 to 2016) and now his son Saša made Oslavia's other legendary skin-contact whites: Ribolla, Jakot (Tokaj spelled backwards, after the EU banned the Tocai name) and Oslavje, macerated for months, aged in large casks, bottled without sulphur in 500 ml bottles with narrow corks he designed.

sites.name: La Castellada
sites.text: The Bensa brothers' Oslavia estate, another pillar of the skin-contact Ribolla tradition.

sites.name: Oslavia
sites.text: The hamlet of Gorizia on the Slovenian border, a First World War battlefield whose ossuary holds about 57,000 Italian soldiers. Its families (Gravner, Radikon, La Castellada, Primosic, Il Carpino, Fiegl, Dario Prinčič) form an association of Ribolla producers and turned the village into the world capital of orange wine.

sites.name: Schiopetto
sites.text: Mario Schiopetto (1930 to 2003) started bottling in 1965 at Capriva and, inspired by German technology, created the clean, varietal Friulian white style that changed Italian winemaking.

sites.name: Russiz Superiore
sites.text: The Marco Felluga family's Capriva estate, on hills once owned by the Counts Strassoldo.

sites.name: Villa Russiz
sites.text: Founded in 1869 by the French count Théodore de La Tour and his Austrian wife Elvine Ritter, who brought French varieties to Collio; since 1919 run by a charitable foundation for orphaned children.

sites.name: Castello di Spessa
sites.text: A castle at Capriva where Giacomo Casanova is said to have stayed in 1773, now a hotel and winery with an 18th-century cellar under the ramparts.

sites.name: Edi Keber
sites.text: Zegla estate near Cormons that makes only one wine, Collio Bianco, from Friulano, Malvasia and Ribolla; Keber championed the idea of a single native-grape Collio white.

sites.name: Jermann
sites.text: Silvio Jermann's Vintage Tunina (first made in 1975), a white blend named after Casanova's maid-lover in his memoirs, became one of Italy's first cult whites. The winery at Ruttars, Dolegna del Collio.

sites.name: Venica & Venica
sites.text: The Venica family estate at Cerò, Dolegna del Collio, farming since 1930; its Sauvignon Ronco delle Mele became one of the most celebrated Italian Sauvignons.

sites.name: Livio Felluga
sites.text: Livio Felluga (1914 to 2016), 'the patriarch of Friulian wine', replanted the abandoned hills of Rosazzo after the war; his Terre Alte white blend (1981) and his map labels are icons.

sites.name: Abbazia di Rosazzo
sites.text: Benedictine abbey on a hilltop above Manzano, a centre of viticulture since the Middle Ages where the last Pignolo vines survived; the Rosazzo DOCG takes its name from it.

sites.name: Rocca Bernarda
sites.text: A 16th-century castle estate near Premariacco where Giuseppe Perusini revived Picolit in the 20th century; later left to the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, which owns it today.

sites.name: Ronchi di Cialla
sites.text: Paolo and Dina Rapuzzi's estate in the Cialla valley, where from 1970 they rescued Schioppettino, helping get it officially authorised in the late 1970s.

sites.name: Le Due Terre
sites.text: Flavio Basilicata and Silvana Forte's tiny Prepotto estate, cult makers of Sacrisassi red and white blends.

sites.name: Miani
sites.text: Enzo Pontoni's tiny Buttrio estate, whose extremely low-yield Friulano and Ribolla are among Italy's most sought-after whites.

sites.name: Vodopivec
sites.text: Paolo Vodopivec's Vitovska-only estate at Sgonico on the Carso, fermented in buried Georgian amphorae.

sites.name: Zidarich
sites.text: Benjamin Zidarich's estate at Prepotto (Praprot) in Duino Aurisina, with a multi-level cellar carved 20 m into the karst rock.

sites.name: Skerk
sites.text: Sandi Skerk's Prepotto estate on the Carso, maker of skin-contact Vitovska and Malvasia from cellars cut into the limestone.

sites.name: Vie di Romans
sites.text: Gianfranco Gallo's Mariano del Friuli estate, which showed that the Isonzo plain could make whites of great power and age-worthiness.

sites.name: Basilica di Aquileia
sites.text: The patriarchal basilica of the Roman city of Aquileia, whose fourth-century mosaic floor, one of the largest in the Christian world, includes scenes of vine harvesting.

sites.name: Ramandolo
sites.text: The hamlet above Nimis at the foot of Monte Bernadia where steep terraces of Verduzzo give the region's oldest sweet-wine DOCG.

sites.name: Vivai Cooperativi Rauscedo
sites.text: The village of Rauscedo in Pordenone province, home of one of the world's largest grapevine nurseries, a cooperative founded in the 1930s that supplies grafted vines to vineyards worldwide.

sites.name: Modigliana
sites.text: The highest, coolest and most forested subzone (180 to 570 m), on the marnoso-arenacea (marl-sandstone) of three valleys, the Ibola, Acerreta and Tramazzo; its pale, tense, perfumed Sangiovese has become the cult corner of Romagna.

sites.name: Predappio
sites.text: Calcareous Pliocene clays (red and grey) at 120 to 400 m in the Rabbi valley, giving silky, ripe tannins; Fattoria Nicolucci (estate since 1880) and Noelia Ricci are references.

sites.name: Bertinoro
sites.text: The 'balcony of Romagna' above Forlì and Cesena, 100 to 350 m, on light clay-loam with limestone and the yellow spungone sandstone; powerful, structured Sangiovese and Albana.

sites.name: Brisighella
sites.text: Spungone and gypsum ridges around the medieval town of three hills (rocca, clock tower and sanctuary), giving fresh, salty Sangiovese.

sites.name: Marzeno
sites.text: The Marzeno valley south of Faenza, home of Fattoria Zerbina, whose Pietramora Riserva and Albana passito made Romagna famous.

sites.name: Oriolo
sites.text: The hills around the hexagonal 15th-century Torre di Oriolo south-east of Faenza, on clays and spungone, giving fresh, mid-weight Sangiovese.

sites.name: Serra
sites.text: The westernmost subzone in the Imola hills of Bologna province around Serra and Castel del Rio.

sites.name: Castrocaro
sites.text: Hills around the spa town of Castrocaro Terme and Terra del Sole, on spungone and clay.

sites.name: Meldola
sites.text: The Bidente valley around Meldola, south of Forlì, a cooler inland subzone of clay and sandstone hills.

sites.name: Cesena
sites.text: Hills south of Cesena in the Savio valley on clays and sands, near the Adriatic, giving rounder, riper Sangiovese.

sites.name: San Vicino
sites.text: The small hills between the Savio and Rubicone around San Vicinio, near the coast.

sites.name: Longiano
sites.text: The easternmost subzone, the hills around the castle of Longiano near the Rubicon.

sites.name: Colonna dell'Ospitalità, Bertinoro
sites.text: The 'Column of Hospitality' in Bertinoro's main square, where noble families competed to host travellers: the ring a traveller tied his horse to decided which family would host him. Bertinoro calls itself the 'city of wine and hospitality'.

sites.name: Rocca di Bertinoro
sites.text: The hilltop fortress of Bertinoro with views from the Apennines to the Adriatic, overlooking the Albana and Sangiovese vineyards.

sites.name: Fattoria Zerbina
sites.text: Cristina Geminiani's Marzeno estate, whose botrytised Albana passito Scacco Matto and Sangiovese Pietramora helped prove Romagna's quality from the late 1980s.

sites.name: Tre Monti
sites.text: The Navacchia family's estate in the Imola hills, known for skin-contact Albana and organic Sangiovese.

sites.name: Cleto Chiarli
sites.text: Founded in Modena in 1860 by Cleto Chiarli, often called the oldest Lambrusco house; its Tenuta Cialdini at Castelvetro and Sorbara Vecchia Modena Premium are references.

sites.name: Cantina di Sorbara
sites.text: The cooperative of Lambrusco di Sorbara's home village between the Secchia and Panaro.

sites.name: Paltrinieri
sites.text: Alberto Paltrinieri's estate at Cristo di Sorbara, a leader in serious dry Sorbara (Radice ancestral method, Leclisse).

sites.name: La Stoppa
sites.text: Elena Pantaleoni's estate at Rivergaro in the Trebbia valley, whose skin-macerated Ageno and long-aged Barbera and Bonarda (Macchiona) are natural-wine landmarks.

sites.name: Castello di Vigoleno
sites.text: The walled medieval village in the Arda valley that gives its name to the rare Vin Santo di Vigoleno.

sites.name: Castelvetro di Modena
sites.text: The hill village whose checkerboard piazza and Rangoni castle overlook the Grasparossa vineyards.
